questions.q: Which statement correctly describes how AI, machine learning (ML), deep learning, and generative AI relate to each other?
options: Generative AI is a subset of deep learning, which is a subset of ML, which is a subset of AI.
AI is a subset of ML, which is a subset of deep learning, which includes generative AI.
ML and deep learning are separate fields, and generative AI belongs to neither of them.
Deep learning is a subset of generative AI, and both sit inside ML, which is one branch of AI.
notes: Correct. Each field nests inside the previous one: GenAI models (such as LLMs) are built with deep neural networks, deep learning is one family of ML methods, and ML is one way to build AI.
Reversed. AI is the broadest field; ML sits inside it, not the other way round.
Deep learning is a branch of ML, and modern generative AI is built on deep learning.
Reversed. Generative AI is one application of deep learning, not its parent.
questions.explain: Think of nested circles: AI (any technique that makes machines act intelligently) contains ML (systems that learn patterns from data), which contains deep learning (ML with many-layered neural networks), which contains generative AI (deep learning models that create new content).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.2; AWS 'What is artificial intelligence?' overview

questions.q: A data science team has finished training a model. The model is now used to score new loan applications as they arrive. What is this second activity called?
options: Feature engineering
Inferencing
Hyperparameter tuning
Data labeling
notes: Feature engineering prepares input variables before training; it does not score new data.
Correct. Inference means using a trained model to make predictions on new, unseen data.
Hyperparameter tuning searches for the best training settings, which happens before deployment.
Labeling adds target values to training data; it is not how predictions are produced.
questions.explain: Training is when a model learns patterns from data. Inferencing is when that trained model is used to produce predictions (or generated output) for new inputs. On AWS, inference can be real-time, batch, asynchronous, or serverless.

questions.q: A media company runs a computer vision model on uploaded videos. Each request carries a payload of several hundred megabytes and takes up to 20 minutes to process. Users are happy to be notified when results are ready. Which Amazon SageMaker AI inference option fits best?
options: Real-time inference
Serverless inference
Asynchronous inference
Batch transform with a nightly schedule
notes: Real-time endpoints are built for low-latency responses with small payloads, not 20-minute jobs.
Serverless inference suits intermittent traffic with small payloads and short processing times.
Correct. Asynchronous inference queues requests, accepts large payloads (up to 1 GB) and long processing times (up to an hour), and notifies you when output is ready.
Batch transform processes a whole dataset offline; it does not respond to each upload as it arrives.
questions.explain: Asynchronous inference is designed for requests with large payloads and long processing times where an immediate answer is not needed. Requests are queued, results land in Amazon S3, and an Amazon SNS notification can tell the caller the job is done. It can also scale the endpoint to zero when idle.
questions.ref: SageMaker AI docs: Asynchronous inference; exam guide skill 1.1.3

questions.q: A startup's internal document classifier gets a few small requests in the morning and then sits idle for hours. Callers need the result returned in the response to their request. The team wants to pay nothing while idle and does not want to manage instances, and a short delay on the first request after an idle period is acceptable. Which inference option should they use?
options: Serverless inference
Real-time inference on a GPU instance
Asynchronous inference with SNS
Batch transform
notes: Correct. Serverless inference scales to zero between requests and you pay only for compute used; the trade-off is cold-start latency.
A real-time endpoint keeps instances running (and billing) even when idle.
Asynchronous inference queues requests and delivers results later to S3, so callers do not get the result in their response; it is meant for large, long-running jobs.
Batch transform runs offline jobs over a dataset; it cannot answer individual requests on demand.
questions.explain: Serverless inference is the fit for intermittent or unpredictable traffic that can tolerate cold starts. AWS provisions and scales the compute for you and scales down to zero when no requests arrive.
questions.ref: SageMaker AI docs: Serverless inference; exam guide skill 1.1.3

questions.q: A retailer wants to score its entire 50-million-row customer table once a week to predict churn. No one needs results instantly, and the team does not want a persistent endpoint. Which inference approach is most suitable?
options: Real-time inference
Batch inference
Serverless inference
Streaming inference on each record
notes: Real-time inference keeps an endpoint running for instant answers, which this job does not need.
Correct. Batch inference (for example, SageMaker AI batch transform) processes a large dataset offline in one job and then shuts down.
Serverless inference handles individual on-demand requests; scoring 50 million rows weekly is a bulk offline job.
Scoring each record through a live stream adds cost and complexity for no benefit here.
questions.explain: Batch inference is used when you have a large set of data to score at once and do not need immediate results. It is usually the cheapest option for periodic bulk scoring because no endpoint runs between jobs.
questions.ref: SageMaker AI docs: Batch transform; exam guide skill 1.1.3

questions.q: Match each workload to the inference type that fits it best.
prompts: Approve or decline a card payment within 100 milliseconds at checkout
Re-score every product in a catalog once each night
Transcribe hour-long recordings that users upload, with results ready later
An HR chatbot used a few times a day that should cost nothing when idle
options: Real-time inference
Batch inference
Asynchronous inference
Serverless inference
questions.explain: Real-time inference serves low-latency, steady traffic. Batch inference scores a whole dataset offline on a schedule. Asynchronous inference queues large or long-running requests and delivers results later. Serverless inference suits sporadic traffic and scales to zero, at the cost of cold starts.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.3; SageMaker AI docs: Deploy models for inference

questions.q: Which dataset is an example of labeled data?
options: 10,000 product photos stored in Amazon S3 with no descriptions
Web server logs collected from an application, stored as raw text
Customer emails, each tagged as 'complaint', 'question', or 'praise'
Raw audio recordings captured from a call center, with no transcripts
notes: Photos without descriptions have no target values, so they are unlabeled.
Raw logs have no attached answers for a model to learn from.
Correct. Each email carries a known target value (its category), which a supervised model can learn to predict.
Recordings without transcripts or tags are unlabeled data.
questions.explain: Labeled data pairs each input with the correct output (the label or target). Supervised learning needs labeled data. Unlabeled data has only inputs and is used for unsupervised learning or for pretraining foundation models.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.4 (labeled and unlabeled data)

questions.q: An energy company records the power consumption of each building every 15 minutes. What type of data is this?
options: Image data
Time-series data
Unlabeled text data
Graph data
notes: There are no images involved, only numeric readings.
Correct. Measurements taken at regular intervals over time form time-series data, which is often used for forecasting.
The readings are numeric values, not text.
Graph data describes relationships between entities (nodes and edges), not readings over time.
questions.explain: Time-series data is a sequence of values recorded in time order, such as sensor readings, stock prices, or website traffic per hour. It is the typical input for forecasting and anomaly detection.

questions.q: Which of the following is unstructured data?
options: A table of orders with order ID, date, and amount columns
Scanned PDF contracts and recorded customer calls
A CSV file of daily exchange rates
A relational database of employee records
notes: A table with fixed columns is structured (tabular) data.
Correct. Documents, images, audio, and video do not follow a fixed row-and-column schema, so they are unstructured.
A CSV with consistent columns is structured data.
Relational tables have a defined schema, which makes them structured.
questions.explain: Structured data fits a predefined schema (rows and columns). Unstructured data, such as text documents, images, audio, and video, has no fixed schema. Most generative AI use cases, such as summarizing documents, work on unstructured data.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.4 (structured and unstructured data)

questions.q: A real estate company has 20 years of past sales with features such as size, location, and age, plus the final sale price of each home. It wants to predict the price of new listings. Which type of learning is this?
options: Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Supervised learning
Self-organizing clustering
notes: Unsupervised learning finds patterns without known answers; here the sale prices are known.
Reinforcement learning learns from rewards through trial and error, not from historical labeled examples.
Correct. The historical sale price is a label, so a model learns the mapping from features to price. Predicting a number makes it a regression task.
Clustering groups similar records without labels; it does not predict a price.
questions.explain: Supervised learning trains on examples where the correct answer is known. Predicting a continuous number (price) is regression; predicting a category is classification. Both are supervised.

questions.q: A marketing team wants to discover natural groups among its customers based on purchase behavior. It has no predefined segments. Which approach fits?
options: Supervised classification
Unsupervised clustering
Reinforcement learning
Linear regression
notes: Classification needs known labels (segments), which the team does not have.
Correct. Clustering is an unsupervised technique that groups similar data points without labels.
Reinforcement learning optimizes actions through rewards; it is not used to find customer segments.
Regression predicts a numeric value and needs labeled training data.
questions.explain: When there are no labels and the goal is to find structure in the data, use unsupervised learning. Clustering (for example, k-means) is the classic way to create customer segments.

questions.q: A logistics company trains a warehouse robot by letting it try different routes. It earns points for fast, collision-free deliveries and loses points for bumps. Over time it learns the best strategy. Which type of learning is this?
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Semi-supervised learning
notes: There is no labeled dataset of correct routes; the robot learns from feedback.
The robot is not grouping data; it is learning which actions maximize a goal.
Correct. In reinforcement learning, an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from rewards and penalties.
Semi-supervised learning mixes a little labeled data with lots of unlabeled data; this robot learns from rewards, not labels.
questions.explain: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains an agent to maximize cumulative reward through trial and error. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) applies the same idea to align foundation models with human preferences.

questions.q: Match each scenario to the type of learning it uses.
prompts: Predict whether an email is spam from 50,000 emails already marked spam or not spam
Find unusual groups of network traffic with no prior examples of attacks
Teach a game-playing agent by giving it a score after every move
options: Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Reinforcement learning
Prompt engineering
questions.explain: Labeled examples mean supervised learning. Finding structure without labels means unsupervised learning. Learning from rewards through interaction means reinforcement learning. Prompt engineering is a way to instruct a foundation model, not a learning type.

questions.q: A model reaches 99% accuracy on its training data but only 62% on new data it has never seen. What is the most likely problem?
options: Underfitting
Overfitting
Data drift since deployment
Too little model complexity
notes: Underfitting means the model performs poorly even on training data, which is not the case here.
Correct. The model has memorized the training data, including noise, and does not generalize. This is high variance.
Drift happens over time in production; this gap appears straight after training.
Too little complexity causes underfitting, the opposite symptom.
questions.explain: Overfitting shows as a large gap between training and test performance. Common fixes are more (or more varied) training data, regularization, early stopping, data augmentation, or a simpler model. Underfitting shows as poor performance on both training and test data.
questions.ref: Exam guide skills 1.1.1 (fit) and 4.1.6 (overfitting and underfitting)

questions.q: In the context of AI, what does 'bias' most commonly refer to?
options: The number of layers and neurons chosen for a neural network architecture
A systematic error that produces unfair or skewed results for certain groups
The randomness setting, such as temperature, used when generating text
The time a model takes to return a prediction after it receives a request
notes: Layer count describes model architecture, not bias.
Correct. Bias in AI usually means systematic skew, often caused by unrepresentative data, that leads to unfair outcomes for some groups.
Randomness in generation is controlled by inference parameters such as temperature.
Response time is latency, not bias.
questions.explain: Bias can enter through training data that under-represents groups, through labels that reflect human prejudice, or through how a model is used. Fairness is the goal of treating groups equitably. Tools such as SageMaker Clarify measure bias in data and models.

questions.q: A factory installs cameras to spot scratches on parts moving along a conveyor belt. Which field of AI does this use?
options: Natural language processing
Computer vision
Speech recognition
Time-series forecasting
notes: NLP works with human language (text), not images.
Correct. Computer vision lets machines interpret images and video, for example to detect defects.
Speech recognition converts spoken audio to text.
Forecasting predicts future values from historical sequences, not defects in images.
questions.explain: Computer vision covers image classification, object detection, and segmentation. On AWS, Amazon Rekognition offers ready-made image and video analysis, and custom models can be trained in SageMaker AI.

questions.q: Which task is a typical natural language processing (NLP) application?
options: Detecting and counting faces in photos uploaded to a website
Determining whether product reviews are positive or negative
Predicting machine failure from vibration sensor readings
Optimizing a delivery route using rewards
notes: Detecting faces is computer vision.
Correct. Sentiment analysis of text is a classic NLP task; Amazon Comprehend offers it as a managed service.
Vibration readings are numeric sensor data, a time-series or anomaly detection problem.
Reward-driven route optimization is reinforcement learning.
questions.explain: NLP lets computers understand, interpret, and generate human language. Common tasks are sentiment analysis, entity recognition, translation, summarization, and question answering.

questions.q: What best distinguishes agentic AI from a standard generative AI chatbot?
options: Agentic AI works only with images and video, while chatbots are limited to working with text.
Agentic AI can plan multi-step tasks, call tools or APIs, and act toward a goal with limited human input.
Agentic AI does not use foundation models; it relies only on hand-written rules and decision trees.
Agentic AI always needs a human to review and approve each response before the user can see it.
notes: Agents can work with any modality; the difference is autonomy and action, not data type.
Correct. An agent reasons about a goal, breaks it into steps, uses tools (APIs, databases, code), and acts, often with memory across steps.
Most AI agents use a foundation model as their reasoning engine.
Human approval can be added, but it is not what defines agentic AI.
questions.explain: A chatbot responds to a prompt. An AI agent pursues a goal: it plans, calls tools, observes results, and iterates. On AWS, agents can be built with Strands Agents or Amazon Bedrock Agents and run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

questions.q: Which statements about deep learning are true? Select TWO.
options: It uses artificial neural networks with many layers.
It can learn useful features directly from raw data such as pixels or text.
It works only on small, structured datasets.
Its decisions are always easy for humans to interpret.
It does not need any training data.
notes: Correct. 'Deep' refers to the many layers of neurons in the network.
Correct. Deep networks learn their own feature representations, which reduces manual feature engineering.
Deep learning shines on large, unstructured datasets such as images, audio, and text.
Deep networks are often hard to interpret, which is why explainability tools exist.
Deep learning typically needs large amounts of training data.
questions.explain: Deep learning uses multi-layer neural networks that learn hierarchical features from raw data. It powers computer vision, speech recognition, and foundation models, but it usually needs lots of data and compute and is harder to explain than simpler models.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.1 (deep learning, neural networks)

questions.q: Which of these are examples of generative AI? Select TWO.
options: Writing product descriptions from a list of features
Classifying credit card transactions as fraud or not fraud
Creating marketing images from a text prompt
Grouping customers into segments with k-means
Predicting next month's sales with a regression model
notes: Correct. The model creates new text that did not exist before.
Fraud classification picks a label from fixed options; it does not create new content.
Correct. Text-to-image models (such as diffusion models) generate new images.
Clustering groups existing records; it creates nothing new.
Regression predicts a number; it is not generative.
questions.explain: Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code. Classification, clustering, and regression analyze or predict from existing data, which is traditional (discriminative) ML.

questions.q: What is the difference between an ML algorithm and an ML model?
options: They are two names for the same thing; both describe the trained file you deploy to an endpoint.
An algorithm is the procedure that learns from data; a model is the trained result, with learned parameters, used to predict.
A model is the step-by-step learning procedure; an algorithm is the weights file saved after training finishes.
An algorithm is used only in deep learning projects, while a model is used only in traditional machine learning work.
notes: They are related but different: one is the method, the other is its output.
Correct. For example, XGBoost is an algorithm; running it on your data produces a model you deploy for inference.
This reverses the two terms.
Both terms apply across all kinds of ML, including deep learning.
questions.explain: An algorithm is the recipe (for example, linear regression or a transformer training procedure). Training applies the algorithm to data and produces a model: an artifact with learned weights that you deploy to make predictions.

questions.q: What is a large language model (LLM)?
options: A rules engine that matches keywords in a question to a library of stored, pre-written answers
A very large neural network, usually transformer-based, trained on vast text to understand and generate language
A database that stores every sentence it was shown and retrieves the closest one word for word
A small model trained only on one company's internal documents, so it has no general knowledge of language
notes: Keyword rules engines are not learned models and cannot generate new language.
Correct. LLMs are foundation models trained on massive text corpora; they predict the next token to generate fluent text.
An LLM learns statistical patterns; it does not store and look up every sentence.
LLMs are trained on broad, very large datasets. Company data is usually added later through RAG or fine-tuning.
questions.explain: LLMs are a type of foundation model specialized in language. They are pretrained on vast text, typically with a transformer architecture, and can be adapted to many tasks through prompting, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), or fine-tuning.

questions.q: Match each system to the category that describes it most precisely.
prompts: A spam filter trained on labeled emails using gradient-boosted trees
An image classifier built from a 50-layer convolutional neural network
A model that writes a product description from a short list of features
An assistant that plans a trip, books flights through APIs, and adjusts when a booking fails
options: Traditional machine learning
Deep learning (non-generative)
Generative AI
Agentic AI
Rules-based automation
questions.explain: Each category narrows the one before it: ML learns from data, deep learning uses many-layered neural networks, generative AI creates new content, and agentic AI adds planning, tool use, and actions toward a goal. Rules-based automation does not learn from data at all.

questions.q: A company stores customer support emails, scanned contracts, and call recordings. Its finance system holds transactions in database tables with fixed columns. How should the two groups of data be classified?
options: Emails, scans, and recordings are unstructured; the transaction tables are structured
All of it is structured, because every file is stored in Amazon S3 or a database
Emails, scans, and recordings are structured; the transaction tables are unstructured
All of it is time-series data, because every record has a timestamp
notes: Correct. Free text, images, and audio have no fixed schema; rows and columns with defined types are structured data.
Where data is stored does not decide its structure. Files in S3 can be completely unstructured.
This reverses the definitions. Tables with fixed columns are the classic example of structured data.
Having a timestamp does not make data time-series. Time-series data is ordered measurements of the same variable over time.
questions.explain: Structured data fits a schema (tables, typed columns) and suits traditional ML. Unstructured data (text, images, audio, video) usually needs deep learning or foundation models. The exam also asks about labeled vs unlabeled, tabular, time-series, image, and text data.

questions.q: A team fine-tunes a model by having it attempt tasks and scoring each attempt with an automated grader that checks whether the final answer is correct, instead of providing a large set of labeled example answers. Which type of learning does this use?
options: Reinforcement learning, guided by a reward signal
Unsupervised learning, because no labels are provided
Supervised learning, because the grader is a kind of label
Transfer learning without any further training
notes: Correct. The model learns from rewards for its own attempts, which is reinforcement learning. RLHF uses human preferences as the reward; other methods use automated graders.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabeled data. Here the model is clearly optimized toward a reward.
Supervised learning needs the correct output for each input. A grader that scores attempts gives a reward, not a target answer.
Transfer learning reuses knowledge from pretraining, but the scenario describes further training driven by rewards.
questions.explain: v1.1 widens 1.1.5 to 'reinforcement learning methods'. Know the family: classic RL (an agent and an environment), RLHF (a reward model trained on human preferences), and reinforcement fine-tuning with automated reward functions, which Amazon Bedrock supports for some models.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.1.5; Amazon Bedrock reinforcement fine-tuning docs

questions.q: Which statements about large language models (LLMs) are true? Select TWO.
options: They are foundation models pretrained on very large amounts of text
They generate output one token at a time by predicting likely next tokens
They look up every answer in a database of verified facts
They must be retrained before they can do any new task
They always return the same answer for the same prompt
notes: Correct. LLMs are a kind of foundation model, pretrained on broad text corpora.
Correct. Generation is next-token prediction, repeated until a stop condition.
LLMs generate from learned patterns. Without grounding such as RAG, they can state false facts.
Prompting, few-shot examples, and RAG adapt LLMs to new tasks without retraining.
With sampling (temperature above zero), outputs vary between runs. This nondeterminism is a known limitation.
questions.explain: v1.1 adds LLM, GenAI, and agentic AI to the basic terms. An LLM is a transformer-based foundation model for language; it adapts to tasks through prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning, and its sampled outputs are nondeterministic.

questions.q: A payroll team wants software that calculates each employee's income tax using the exact formula set by law. Every result must be identical for identical inputs. What is the best approach?
options: Train a regression model on past payslips
Use a generative AI model to estimate the tax for each employee
Implement the formula as deterministic rules in code
Cluster employees by salary band and use averages
notes: A regression model only approximates past results and can be wrong for edge cases.
Generative models are probabilistic and can give different answers to the same input.
Correct. When the rules are known and an exact, repeatable outcome is required, ML adds cost and risk without benefit.
Averages per cluster would give wrong amounts for individuals.
questions.explain: AI/ML is not appropriate when a problem has a known, exact solution or must produce one deterministic answer. ML predictions are probabilistic, so a rules-based program is cheaper and more reliable for fixed formulas.

questions.q: A company has 2,000 policy documents. Employees want to ask questions in plain language and get answers that cite the right document. Which AI application best fits?
options: An image classification model trained on scans of every document page
A knowledge base that retrieves relevant passages for an LLM to answer from
A clustering model that groups the documents by their length and age
A reinforcement learning agent that is rewarded each time it gives a short answer
notes: The documents are text; image classification would not answer questions.
Correct. A knowledge base with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), such as Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, finds relevant passages and lets the model answer with citations.
Grouping by length does nothing to answer employees' questions.
Rewarding short answers would not make them accurate or grounded in the documents.
questions.explain: Question answering over company documents is one of the most common generative AI applications. A knowledge base stores document chunks as embeddings, retrieves the most relevant ones for each question, and passes them to an FM so the answer is grounded and can cite sources.

questions.q: An insurer receives 40,000 claims a day and wants to flag the ones that need a human adjuster. What main value does ML add here?
options: It removes the need for any human to review claims at all
It guarantees that every single flag it raises is correct
It scales decision support to a volume people cannot review quickly
It makes the whole claims process fully deterministic and rule-based
notes: ML helps prioritize; humans still review flagged and borderline cases.
ML predictions are probabilistic and will sometimes be wrong.
Correct. ML can triage huge volumes consistently and quickly, so adjusters focus on the claims that need them.
ML outputs are probabilistic, not deterministic rules.
questions.explain: AI/ML adds value through decision support, scalability, and automation, for example by triaging large volumes so people can focus on high-value work. It does not guarantee correctness, so human oversight remains important.

questions.q: A subscription business wants to predict whether each customer will cancel in the next 30 days (yes or no). Which ML technique fits?
options: Regression
Binary classification
Clustering
Dimensionality reduction
notes: Regression predicts a continuous number, not a yes/no outcome.
Correct. Predicting one of two categories (will cancel / will not) is binary classification.
Clustering groups unlabeled data; it does not predict a known outcome.
Dimensionality reduction compresses features; it does not make the prediction itself.
questions.explain: Classification predicts a category (binary for two classes, multiclass for more). Regression predicts a number. Clustering finds groups without labels. Churn prediction is a textbook binary classification problem.

questions.q: A food delivery app wants to predict how many minutes each order will take to arrive. Which technique should it use?
options: Classification
Clustering
Regression
Topic modeling
notes: Classification picks a category; delivery time is a continuous number.
Clustering finds groups and does not predict a target value.
Correct. Predicting a continuous numeric value such as minutes is regression.
Topic modeling finds themes in text documents.
questions.explain: Use regression when the target is a quantity: price, time, temperature, demand. Linear regression and gradient-boosted trees (such as XGBoost) are common choices.

questions.q: Match each business problem to the ML technique that fits it.
prompts: Estimate the monthly electricity bill for a household
Decide whether a loan application is high risk or low risk
Group 10,000 news articles by theme with no labels
options: Regression
Classification
Clustering
Reinforcement learning
questions.explain: A numeric target means regression; a category means classification; finding groups without labels means clustering. Reinforcement learning is for learning actions through rewards, which none of these problems need.

questions.q: A call center wants written transcripts of every recorded customer call. Which AWS service should it use?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Translate
Amazon Lex
notes: Polly does the opposite: it turns text into speech.
Correct. Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text and offers features such as speaker identification, custom vocabulary, and PII redaction.
Translate converts text from one language to another; it does not process audio.
Lex builds conversational bots; it is not a batch transcription service.
questions.explain: Amazon Transcribe is automatic speech recognition (ASR) as a managed service. Transcribe Call Analytics adds call-center insights such as sentiment and call summaries.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.2.5; Amazon Transcribe overview

questions.q: A hotel chain wants a chatbot on its website that understands requests such as 'book a room for two nights' and asks follow-up questions for missing details. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Polly
Amazon Lex
Amazon Textract
notes: Comprehend analyzes text (sentiment, entities) but does not manage a conversation.
Polly only converts text to speech.
Correct. Amazon Lex builds voice and text chatbots using intents, sample utterances, and slots, and prompts users for missing slot values.
Textract extracts text and data from documents.
questions.explain: Amazon Lex provides conversational interfaces. An intent is what the user wants (BookRoom); slots are the details needed (dates, guests). Lex can fulfill the request by calling AWS Lambda.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.2.5; Amazon Lex overview

questions.q: A news app wants to offer an audio version of every article, read in a natural-sounding voice. Which AWS service should it use?
options: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
notes: Transcribe converts speech into text, the opposite direction.
Correct. Amazon Polly is text-to-speech with lifelike neural voices and SSML for controlling pronunciation and pauses.
Rekognition analyzes images and video.
Comprehend analyzes the meaning of text but does not produce audio.
questions.explain: Polly turns text into speech. Remember the pair: Transcribe = speech to text, Polly = text to speech.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.2.5; Amazon Polly overview

questions.q: An online store wants its product catalog available in 12 languages, using its own approved terms for brand and product names. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon Translate with custom terminology
Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabulary
Amazon Polly with lexicons
Amazon Comprehend with custom entities
notes: Correct. Amazon Translate does neural machine translation, and custom terminology keeps brand and product names consistent.
Transcribe works on audio; custom vocabulary improves speech recognition, not translation.
Polly lexicons control pronunciation in speech; they do not translate text.
Comprehend custom entities find terms in text; they do not translate it.
questions.explain: Amazon Translate handles real-time and batch translation. Custom terminology tells it exactly how to translate (or not translate) specific terms such as brand names.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.2.5; Amazon Translate custom terminology

questions.q: A product team wants to know which product features customers mention most in 100,000 reviews and whether each review is positive or negative. Which managed service provides this with no ML expertise?
options: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Personalize
Amazon Textract
notes: Rekognition analyzes images and video, not review text.
Correct. Amazon Comprehend detects sentiment, key phrases, entities, and language in text, and can run topic modeling over a collection of documents.
Personalize generates recommendations from user behavior.
Textract extracts text from scanned documents; it does not judge sentiment.
questions.explain: Amazon Comprehend is the managed NLP service for insights from text. Typical uses are sentiment analysis, entity recognition, key phrase extraction, PII detection, and custom classification.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.2.5; Amazon Comprehend features

questions.q: An accounts payable team receives thousands of scanned invoices. It needs the vendor name, the totals, and every line-item table extracted automatically. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Textract
Amazon Translate
notes: Comprehend analyzes text that already exists; it does not read scanned images.
Rekognition can find text in images but does not understand forms and tables.
Correct. Amazon Textract extracts printed and handwritten text, form key-value pairs, and tables from documents, and has a dedicated invoice and receipt analysis API.
Translate converts text between languages.
questions.explain: Textract goes beyond simple OCR: it understands document structure such as forms, tables, and queries, which is what invoice processing needs.

questions.q: A video streaming service wants to show each viewer 'recommended for you' titles based on their viewing history, without building ML models itself. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon Personalize
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Lex
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
notes: Correct. Amazon Personalize builds real-time recommendation models from interaction data, using the same kind of technology Amazon.com uses.
Comprehend analyzes text; it does not recommend items.
Lex builds chatbots.
Ground Truth labels training data; it does not make recommendations.
questions.explain: Amazon Personalize is a managed recommender service. You provide users, items, and interactions; it trains models for use cases such as personalized recommendations, similar items, and personalized ranking.

questions.q: A social media startup must automatically detect explicit or violent images before they are published. Which AWS service provides this as a ready-made API?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Polly
Amazon Comprehend
notes: Textract extracts text and data from documents.
Correct. Amazon Rekognition content moderation detects inappropriate, unwanted, or offensive content in images and videos.
Polly converts text to speech.
Comprehend analyzes text, not images.
questions.explain: Amazon Rekognition offers pretrained computer vision APIs: object and scene detection, face analysis, text in images, and content moderation. Uncertain results can be routed to human reviewers with Amazon Augmented AI (A2I).

questions.q: Match each requirement to the AWS AI service built for it.
prompts: Turn recorded meetings into text
Read an article aloud in a lifelike voice
Convert support articles from English to Japanese
Find the people, places, and sentiment in customer emails
Build a chatbot that books appointments
options: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
Amazon Translate
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Lex
questions.explain: Transcribe: speech to text. Polly: text to speech. Translate: language to language. Comprehend: insights from text. Lex: conversational bots. These task-specific services need no ML expertise.

questions.q: A company wants to analyze the sentiment of its recorded support calls with as little custom development as possible. Which two AWS services should it combine? Select TWO.
options: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Polly
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Personalize
notes: Correct. Transcribe turns the call audio into text first.
Correct. Comprehend then detects sentiment in the transcribed text.
Polly generates speech; this pipeline needs to understand speech.
Rekognition analyzes images and video, not audio.
Personalize makes recommendations; it does not analyze sentiment.
questions.explain: A common pattern chains managed services: Transcribe (speech to text), then Comprehend (sentiment, entities, key phrases). Transcribe Call Analytics can also report sentiment directly for call-center audio.

questions.q: A bank builds a credit-approval model. Regulators require the bank to explain the main reasons behind every individual decision, and the inputs are structured application data. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A general-purpose LLM that reads each application and decides
A traditional ML model on the tabular data, with feature-attribution explanations
A diffusion model that generates a personalized approval letter
A chatbot that asks each applicant to rate their own credit risk on a scale of one to ten
notes: LLM decisions are harder to explain and less consistent, which is a problem under strict regulation.

Correct. Traditional ML (for example, gradient-boosted trees or logistic regression) works well on tabular data, is cheaper, and can be explained per decision, for example with SageMaker Clarify SHAP values.
Generating a letter does not make or justify the credit decision.
Self-rated risk is neither reliable nor a model-based decision.
questions.explain: Version 1.1 of the guide asks when traditional ML beats a foundation model. Regulatory, explainability, and operational constraints (cost, latency, consistency) often favor traditional ML for structured prediction tasks. FMs shine on open-ended language and content tasks.

questions.q: A support team wants to summarize long, free-text customer tickets and draft a suggested reply for each. Which approach fits best?
options: A foundation model accessed through a managed service such as Amazon Bedrock
A linear regression model trained on the length of past tickets
A k-means clustering model that sorts the tickets into five groups
A rules engine that returns one fixed, pre-written reply for each keyword it detects
notes: Correct. Summarization and drafting replies are open-ended language generation tasks that FMs handle well without training a custom model.
Regression predicts numbers; it cannot write summaries.
Clustering could group tickets but cannot summarize or draft replies.
Fixed keyword replies cannot adapt to the details of each ticket.
questions.explain: Foundation models are the right tool for unstructured, open-ended tasks such as summarization, drafting, and question answering. Amazon Bedrock offers FMs through an API, so there is no infrastructure to manage.

questions.q: In which situations is a traditional ML model usually a better choice than a foundation model? Select TWO.
options: Each decision must be explainable to a regulator in terms of input features
Millions of low-latency predictions per day on structured tabular data at minimal cost
The task is to write personalized marketing emails in several languages
Users ask open-ended questions about a large set of unstructured documents
The team needs one model to handle many different language tasks with no training
notes: Correct. Simpler models on tabular features are far easier to explain decision by decision.
Correct. A small purpose-built model is cheaper, faster, and more predictable at high volume than calling a large FM.
Writing varied, multilingual emails is a generative language task suited to an FM.
Open-ended questions over documents suit an FM with RAG.
Handling many tasks with no training is a key strength of foundation models.
questions.explain: Choose traditional ML when you need explainability, regulatory comfort, low cost per prediction, low latency, and consistent outputs on structured data. Choose FMs for unstructured content, generation, and flexibility across many tasks.

questions.q: A small bakery gets about 20 online orders a week and wants to 'use AI' to forecast demand. It has three months of sales history. What is the most reasonable advice?
options: Train a large custom deep learning model on SageMaker AI right away
Fine-tune a foundation model on the three months of sales records
Weigh the cost and data needs first; simple averages or spreadsheet trends may be enough
Skip collecting any data and let a generative model guess each week's demand from scratch
notes: Very little data and low volume make a custom deep learning model expensive overkill.
Fine-tuning an FM on a tiny sales table adds cost without giving a reliable forecast.
Correct. A cost-benefit check comes first. With little data and low stakes, a simple method may beat an ML project on value.
Guessing without data gives no reliable basis for decisions.
questions.explain: AI/ML is not always appropriate. Consider cost versus benefit, whether you have enough quality data, and whether a simpler non-ML solution meets the need. Sometimes the right answer is not to use ML.

questions.q: A manufacturer wants to run defect detection on cameras inside a factory that has an unreliable internet connection. Each prediction must take under 20 milliseconds and cost almost nothing. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: A small, purpose-trained computer vision model deployed close to the cameras
A large multimodal foundation model called through a cloud API for every image
A text-generation model that writes a description of each part
A human inspector who checks a random sample of parts once a week
notes: Correct. Operational constraints such as latency, connectivity, and cost per prediction favor a small, specialized model running locally.
A large FM over the internet adds latency and cost and fails when the connection drops.
Generating text does not detect defects reliably or quickly.
Weekly sampling would miss most defects and does not meet the real-time need.
questions.explain: New objective 1.2.6: choose traditional ML over FMs when regulation, explainability, or operational constraints (latency, cost, offline operation, consistency) demand it. Choose FMs for open-ended language and content tasks.

questions.q: A credit card company has very few confirmed fraud labels, and fraud patterns change often. It wants to flag transactions that look very different from a customer's normal behavior. Which ML approach fits best?
options: Unsupervised anomaly detection
Linear regression on transaction amounts
A text-to-image diffusion model
Supervised classification trained only on the few existing labels
notes: Correct. Anomaly detection learns what normal looks like and flags outliers, so it works with few labels and catches new patterns.
Regression predicts a number. It does not flag unusual behavior.
Diffusion models generate images. They do not detect fraud.
With very few labels and changing patterns, a purely supervised model would miss new kinds of fraud.
questions.explain: Fraud detection is a listed real-world AI application. When labels are scarce or patterns shift, unsupervised anomaly detection (for example, Random Cut Forest in SageMaker AI) complements supervised classification.

questions.q: An IT department wants an assistant that reads a ticket, looks up the user in the directory, resets the password through an API, and closes the ticket, asking a human only when something is unclear. Which kind of AI application is this?
options: Agentic AI
Time-series forecasting
Image classification
Clustering
notes: Correct. The assistant pursues a goal across several steps, calls tools, and acts on systems, which is agentic AI.
Forecasting predicts future values from historical data. It does not take actions.
Image classification labels images. Nothing here involves images.
Clustering groups similar items. It does not carry out a workflow.
questions.explain: v1.1 adds knowledge bases and agentic AI to the real-world AI applications in skill 1.2.4. Agents suit multi-step, tool-using tasks with some judgment; keep humans involved where actions are risky or unclear.

questions.q: A company is deciding whether to use ML at all. Which situations suggest that an ML solution is NOT appropriate? Select TWO.
options: A regulation requires one exact, auditable result for each input
The expected benefit is smaller than the cost of collecting data and running the model
There are millions of records with useful patterns that humans cannot review
The task involves understanding free-form customer messages
Decisions must scale far beyond what the current staff can handle
notes: Correct. When a specific, deterministic outcome is required, rules or code are a better fit than probabilistic predictions.
Correct. A cost-benefit analysis can show that ML is not worth it.
Large volumes with hidden patterns are a classic reason to use ML.
Understanding free text is a strength of NLP and foundation models.
Scaling decision support is one of the main values of ML.
questions.explain: Skill 1.2.2 asks when AI/ML is not appropriate: when the cost outweighs the benefit, or when a specific outcome is needed instead of a prediction. Skill 1.2.1 lists where it adds value: decision support, scalability, and automation.

questions.q: Put these stages of a typical ML pipeline in the right order.
options: Collect the data
Clean the data and engineer features
Train and tune the model
Evaluate the model on held-out data
Deploy the model and monitor it in production
questions.explain: A typical pipeline runs: data collection, then preparation (exploratory analysis, cleaning, feature engineering), then training and hyperparameter tuning, then evaluation on data the model has not seen, then deployment with ongoing monitoring. Monitoring results often feed back into retraining.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.3.1 (components of an AI/ML pipeline)

questions.q: What is the main purpose of exploratory data analysis (EDA) in an ML project?
options: To deploy a first version of the model to a production endpoint as early as possible, then improve it
To understand the data's distributions, missing values, outliers, and correlations before modeling
To choose the instance type that will host the final model endpoint
To measure the trained model's accuracy, precision, and recall on the test set after training finishes
notes: Deployment happens much later, after training and evaluation.
Correct. EDA uses statistics and charts to understand the data and spot quality problems before you build features and train.
Instance selection is a deployment concern, not part of EDA.
Measuring accuracy is model evaluation, which comes after training.
questions.explain: EDA is an early pipeline stage. It reveals data quality issues (missing values, outliers, class imbalance) and relationships between variables that guide cleaning and feature engineering.

questions.q: A team turns a raw 'signup_timestamp' column into new inputs such as 'day of week' and 'days since signup' to help a churn model. What is this step called?
options: Hyperparameter tuning
Feature engineering
Model monitoring
Inference
notes: Hyperparameter tuning adjusts training settings such as learning rate, not the input columns.
Correct. Feature engineering creates, transforms, or selects input variables so the model can learn more easily.
Monitoring watches a deployed model's behavior over time.
Inference is using a trained model to make predictions.
questions.explain: Features are the inputs a model learns from. Good feature engineering, such as extracting date parts, scaling numbers, or encoding categories, often improves a model more than changing the algorithm.

questions.q: Which of the following is a hyperparameter rather than a model parameter?
options: The learning rate chosen before training starts
The weights a neural network learns during training
The coefficients a linear regression model learns from data
The bias terms that are adjusted on every training step
notes: Correct. Hyperparameters, such as learning rate, number of epochs, or tree depth, are set before training and control how learning happens.
Weights are parameters the model learns from the data.
Coefficients are learned parameters.
Bias terms are learned parameters, updated during training.
questions.explain: Parameters are learned from data during training. Hyperparameters are chosen by people (or by automated tuning, such as SageMaker AI automatic model tuning) before training. Tuning searches for the hyperparameters that give the best validation performance.

questions.q: A company wants to add text summarization to its app quickly, with minimal ML expertise and no infrastructure to manage. Which way of getting a foundation model fits best?
options: Train a new foundation model from scratch on company data
Call a pretrained foundation model through a managed API such as Amazon Bedrock
Collect and label a million example summaries, then train a custom summarization model on them
Hire a research team to design a new model architecture
notes: Training an FM from scratch takes huge datasets, specialist skills, and a large budget.
Correct. A managed API gives immediate access to pretrained FMs with no servers to run.
Building a labeled dataset and training a custom model is slow and costly compared with using an existing FM.
Designing a new architecture is research work that is unnecessary for summarization.
questions.explain: FMs can come from pretrained models (proprietary or open source, available through Amazon Bedrock or SageMaker JumpStart) or from custom training. For most business needs, starting from a pretrained model is far faster and cheaper.

questions.q: A regulated company wants to run an open-source LLM. It must control the exact model weights, the instance type, and the network the endpoint runs in. Which production approach fits?
options: Use a consumer chatbot website in a browser
Self-host the model on an Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint inside its own VPC
Copy the model weights to an Amazon S3 Glacier archive
Call a third-party API that gives no control over where its data is processed or stored
notes: A consumer website gives no control over weights, infrastructure, or data handling.

Correct. Self-hosting, for example by deploying from SageMaker JumpStart to a SageMaker AI endpoint, gives control over the model version, compute, and networking, at the cost of more operational work.
Glacier is archival storage; it cannot serve inference.
A third-party API removes the control the company needs.
questions.explain: There are two main ways to use a model in production: a managed API (least effort, less control, such as Amazon Bedrock) or a self-hosted API (more control and more operational responsibility, such as a SageMaker AI endpoint).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.3.3 (managed API vs self-hosted API)

questions.q: A developer wants an AI-powered IDE that turns a feature request into requirements, a design, and a task list, and then helps implement the code. Which AWS offering is built for this spec-driven style of development?
options: Kiro
Amazon Quick
Strands Agents
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
notes: Correct. Kiro is an agentic IDE built around spec-driven development: requirements, design, and tasks before code.
Amazon Quick is for business users (analytics, research, automation), not for writing software.
Strands Agents is an SDK for coding your own agents. It is not an IDE that turns feature requests into specs.
AgentCore hosts and operates agents in production. It does not write application code for developers.
questions.explain: Kiro, added to the exam guide in v1.1, is an AI development environment. It uses specs, steering files, and agent hooks to help developers go from prompt to production code in a structured way.
questions.ref: Exam guide skills 1.3.4 and 2.3.1 (v1.1); Kiro documentation

questions.q: Business analysts want to build dashboards, ask questions about their data in natural language, and automate simple research tasks, without writing code. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Quick
AWS Lambda
Amazon EMR
notes: SageMaker AI is a platform for data scientists to build, train, and deploy models.
Correct. Amazon Quick (Quick Suite) brings BI dashboards (Quick Sight), natural-language Q&A, research, and workflow automation together for business users.
Lambda runs code; it is not an analytics tool for business users.
EMR runs big-data frameworks such as Spark and needs engineering skills.
questions.explain: Amazon Quick is the agentic workspace for business users, building on what was Amazon QuickSight. In the v1.1 guide it appears as an AWS service for AI-powered analytics and generative AI applications.

questions.q: Match each AWS service to its main role in building AI solutions.
prompts: Access many foundation models through one managed API
Build, train, and deploy custom ML models with full control
Agentic IDE that helps developers write code from specs
Analytics, dashboards, and AI agents for business users
Modernize legacy .NET, mainframe, and VMware workloads with AI agents
options: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker AI
Kiro
Amazon Quick
AWS Transform
Amazon Comprehend
questions.explain: Bedrock gives managed access to FMs, SageMaker AI is the full ML platform, Kiro is the agentic IDE, Amazon Quick serves business users with analytics and agents, and AWS Transform applies agentic AI to modernization. Amazon Comprehend is a task-specific NLP service and fits none of these.

questions.q: Six months after launch, a team cannot reproduce how its current model was trained, because the data, code, and settings were never recorded. Which MLOps practice would have prevented this?
options: Using a larger instance type for training jobs
Versioning data, code, and models and tracking experiments in an automated pipeline
Increasing the number of training epochs on every run
Deploying the model to more AWS Regions at the same time so that copies of it always exist somewhere
notes: Bigger instances make training faster, not reproducible.
Correct. Repeatability comes from versioning everything and running training in tracked, automated pipelines (for example, SageMaker Pipelines, experiment tracking, and a model registry).
More epochs change training results; they do not record how a model was built.
Multi-Region deployment is about availability, not reproducibility.
questions.explain: MLOps applies DevOps ideas to ML: experimentation tracking, repeatability, scalability, managing technical debt, production readiness, monitoring, and retraining. Versioned, automated pipelines make every model traceable and reproducible.

questions.q: A demand-forecasting model was accurate at launch, but its errors have grown steadily over a year as customer habits changed. What should the team put in place?
options: Stop collecting new data to keep the model stable
Monitor the model in production for drift and retrain it on recent data
Lower the model's temperature parameter to reduce errors
Delete the old evaluation dataset and then redeploy exactly the same model to a new endpoint
notes: Without new data the model cannot learn the changed patterns.
Correct. Real-world data changes (data and concept drift). Monitoring catches the decline, and retraining on recent data restores accuracy.
Temperature is a generation setting for foundation models; it does not fix a drifting forecast model.
Redeploying the same model does nothing about the change in the data.
questions.explain: Models degrade as the world changes. Monitoring and retraining are core MLOps practices. On AWS, model monitoring can detect drift in data quality, model quality, and bias, and pipelines can automate retraining.

questions.q: A team's ML system relies on manual notebook steps, copied code, and undocumented data fixes that only one engineer understands. Which MLOps concept does this describe?
options: Technical debt
Production readiness
Hyperparameter optimization
Transfer learning
notes: Correct. Shortcuts that make a system hard to maintain, reproduce, or change are technical debt; ML systems pile it up quickly.
Production readiness is the goal this system falls short of: reliable, automated, monitored, and secure.
Hyperparameter optimization tunes training settings.
Transfer learning reuses a pretrained model for a new task.
questions.explain: ML technical debt comes from fragile pipelines, hidden dependencies, and manual steps. MLOps reduces it with automation, versioning, testing, and documentation, so systems become production ready and easier to scale.

questions.q: A fraud model is tested on 1,000 transactions. It flags 100 as fraud, and 80 of those really are fraud. There are 120 fraudulent transactions in total. What is the model's precision?
notes: 0.67 is the recall: 80 caught out of 120 actual frauds.
Correct. Precision = true positives / everything flagged = 80 / 100 = 0.80.
0.94 is the accuracy: (80 true positives + 860 true negatives) / 1,000.
0.20 is the share of flags that were wrong (20 false positives out of 100 flagged), the opposite of precision.
questions.explain: Precision = TP / (TP + FP) answers: of the items flagged, how many were right? Here TP = 80 and FP = 20, so precision is 0.80. Recall = TP / (TP + FN) = 80 / 120 ≈ 0.67 answers: of the real frauds, how many were caught?

questions.q: A hospital uses a model to screen scans for a serious disease. Missing a sick patient is far worse than sending a healthy patient for a follow-up test. Which metric should the team prioritize?
options: Precision
Recall
Accuracy
Latency
notes: Precision limits false alarms, but false alarms are the cheaper mistake here.
Correct. Recall measures how many actual positive cases the model catches. High recall means few missed patients (false negatives).
Accuracy can look high even when many sick patients are missed, especially if the disease is rare.
Latency is about speed, not about missed diagnoses.
questions.explain: Prioritize recall when false negatives are costly (disease screening, fraud you must not miss). Prioritize precision when false positives are costly (blocking legitimate emails or payments). F1 balances the two.

questions.q: An email provider's spam filter must almost never send a legitimate message to the spam folder, even if some spam gets through. Which metric matters most?
options: Recall
Precision
Mean squared error
Perplexity
notes: High recall catches more spam but would accept more legitimate emails wrongly flagged.
Correct. Precision = TP / (TP + FP). High precision means that what gets flagged as spam really is spam, so few legitimate emails are lost.
Mean squared error measures regression error, not classification.
Perplexity measures how well a language model predicts text.
questions.explain: When false positives are expensive, optimize precision. Here a false positive is a real email hidden in the spam folder.

questions.q: A classifier has a precision of 0.6 and a recall of 0.9. What is its F1 score?
notes: 0.54 is precision × recall, not F1.
0.75 is the simple average of 0.6 and 0.9; F1 uses the harmonic mean.
0.90 is just the recall.
questions.explain: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: 2PR / (P + R). It is pulled towards the lower of the two values, so a model cannot score well by maximizing only one of them.

questions.q: Only 1% of a bank's transactions are fraudulent. A model that predicts 'not fraud' for every transaction scores 99% accuracy. Why is accuracy misleading here?
options: Because accuracy cannot be computed for classification problems
Because with imbalanced classes the model catches no fraud at all, so recall for fraud is zero
Because 99% accuracy always means the model has overfit its training data
Because accuracy only works for regression problems with continuous outputs, not for classes like fraud
notes: Accuracy is a standard classification metric; it is just uninformative on imbalanced data.
Correct. The model never finds the minority class. Precision, recall, and F1 for the fraud class reveal the problem.
High accuracy does not by itself indicate overfitting; here the model is simply trivial.
Accuracy is a classification metric; regression uses errors such as RMSE.
questions.explain: With class imbalance, accuracy is dominated by the majority class. Evaluate the minority class with precision, recall, and F1, and consider rebalancing the data.

questions.q: Leadership asks whether a new AI customer-service assistant is worth its cost. Which metric answers that business question most directly?
options: F1 score of the intent classifier
Return on investment (ROI)
Training loss on the final epoch
Number of model parameters
notes: F1 measures model quality, not business value.
Correct. ROI compares the value delivered (savings, extra revenue) with the total cost of building and running the solution.
Training loss is a technical signal used during training.
Parameter count describes model size, not value to the business.
questions.explain: The guide separates model metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) from business metrics (cost per user, development cost, customer feedback, ROI). Executives decide on business metrics.

questions.q: Which of these are business metrics for an AI solution, rather than model performance metrics? Select TWO.
options: Cost per user
Customer feedback scores
Recall
Precision
F1 score
notes: Correct. Cost per user tracks the economics of running the solution.
Correct. Customer feedback reflects how users experience the solution.
Recall is a model metric.
Precision is a model metric.
F1 is a model metric.
questions.explain: Model metrics tell you how well the model predicts. Business metrics tell you whether the solution creates value: cost per user, development cost, customer feedback, and ROI.

questions.q: A data science team needs managed notebooks, distributed training jobs, automatic model tuning, and one-click deployment of its own custom models. Which AWS service provides all of these?
options: Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
AWS Glue
notes: Correct. SageMaker AI covers notebooks, training jobs, automatic model tuning, and deployment of custom models.
Bedrock gives API access to foundation models. It does not run distributed training of your own model code.
Canvas is a no-code tool for analysts. It does not give data scientists notebooks and distributed training jobs.
AWS Glue prepares and moves data (ETL). It does not train or deploy models.
questions.explain: Amazon SageMaker AI is AWS's end-to-end platform for building, training, and deploying ML models. It also hosts foundation models (SageMaker JumpStart) and tools for responsible AI such as Clarify and Model Cards.

questions.q: Match each ML pipeline need to the Amazon SageMaker AI capability built for it.
prompts: Prepare and transform data visually, with built-in data quality insights
Store curated features and reuse them for both training and inference
Catalog model versions and record approval before deployment
Detect data drift and quality drift on a deployed endpoint
Let business analysts build models without writing code
options: SageMaker Data Wrangler
SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Model Registry
SageMaker Model Monitor
SageMaker Canvas
SageMaker Ground Truth
questions.explain: Map tools to pipeline stages: Data Wrangler (data preparation), Feature Store (feature reuse), training and tuning jobs, Model Registry (versioning and approval), endpoints (deployment), and Model Monitor (monitoring). Canvas offers no-code ML. Ground Truth labels data, which none of these prompts describes.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 1.3.4; Amazon SageMaker AI docs

questions.q: A company must make sure that only models reviewed by the risk team are deployed to production, and it must be able to roll back to an earlier approved version. Which MLOps capability supports this most directly?
options: A model registry with versioning and approval status
A larger training instance type
Raising the number of training epochs on every run
Deleting earlier model versions after each deployment
notes: Correct. A model registry, such as SageMaker Model Registry, tracks versions, metadata, and approval status, and supports rollback.
Instance size affects training speed, not deployment governance.
More epochs change training, not which version is approved for production.
Deleting old versions removes the ability to roll back.
questions.explain: Production readiness in MLOps includes versioned, approved, reproducible models. Pipelines can deploy automatically only after a model is approved in the registry.

questions.q: A retail company wants a generative AI chat feature quickly. It is choosing between calling a model through Amazon Bedrock and hosting an open-weight model on its own endpoints. What is the main trade-off?
options: A managed API means less operational work but less control; self-hosting means more control and more operational work
A managed API always gives more accurate answers than any self-hosted model, whatever the task
Self-hosting removes every security responsibility from the customer and shifts it to AWS
There is no real difference in effort or control between the two options for production use
notes: Correct. This is the core trade-off between using a managed API service and running a self-hosted API.
Accuracy depends on the model, not on whether it is managed or self-hosted.
Self-hosting adds security responsibilities, such as patching and network configuration.
The options differ a lot in operational effort and in control over models and infrastructure.
questions.explain: Skill 1.3.3 contrasts methods to use a model in production: a managed API service (Amazon Bedrock) and a self-hosted API (for example, a SageMaker AI endpoint or Amazon EC2).

questions.q: Put these MLOps activities in the order they usually occur for a model that is already in production.
options: Monitor the deployed model's inputs and predictions
Detect drift above an agreed threshold
Retrain the model on recent data
Evaluate the new model against the current one
Deploy the new version after approval
questions.explain: Production MLOps is a loop: monitor, detect drift, retrain, evaluate against the current model, and redeploy only after approval. Automating this loop with pipelines is what makes it repeatable.

questions.q: In the context of large language models, what is a token?
options: A unit of text, such as a word or part of a word, that the model reads and generates
A password-like secret string that grants an application access to a model's API endpoint
A single complete document stored in a vector database
A security credential that encrypts every prompt before it is sent to the model
notes: Correct. Models split text into tokens (whole words, sub-words, or characters) and both read and produce text one token at a time.
An API key is a credential, not a token in the language-model sense.
Documents are made of many tokens; a token is far smaller.
Encryption keys protect data; they are unrelated to how models process text.
questions.explain: Tokens are the basic units an LLM works with. In English, one token is roughly three-quarters of a word on average. Context windows, limits, and pricing are all measured in tokens.

questions.q: A chatbot sends about 2,000 input tokens and receives about 500 output tokens per request. The model costs $0.003 per 1,000 input tokens and $0.015 per 1,000 output tokens. What is the cost of 10,000 requests?
notes: $60 counts only input tokens: 20 million × $0.003 / 1,000.
$75 counts only output tokens: 5 million × $0.015 / 1,000.
$180 would mean pricing all 25 million tokens at an average that does not match these rates.
questions.explain: With on-demand, token-based pricing you pay separately for input and output tokens, and output tokens usually cost more. Total cost = input tokens × input price + output tokens × output price. Shorter prompts and capped output lengths cut cost directly.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.4 (token-based pricing, new in v1.1)

questions.q: A company's Amazon Bedrock bill is high because every request repeats a 6,000-token instruction block. Which actions reduce cost per request? Select TWO.
options: Use prompt caching for the repeated instruction block
Trim the instructions and cap the maximum output tokens
Raise the temperature so answers are more creative
Switch from on-demand to a larger, more capable model
Add more few-shot examples to every prompt
notes: Correct. Prompt caching lets the model reuse a repeated prompt prefix, which cuts the cost and latency of those cached input tokens.
Correct. Fewer input tokens and a sensible output cap directly reduce billed tokens.
Temperature changes randomness, not the number of tokens billed.
Larger models usually cost more per token, not less.
Extra examples add input tokens and raise cost.
questions.explain: Token-based pricing rewards lean prompts. Prompt caching (for repeated context), shorter instructions, output limits, smaller models for simple tasks, and batch inference for non-urgent work all reduce cost.

questions.q: Users complain that a generative AI assistant takes a long time to finish long answers. Why does output length affect latency so strongly?
options: The model generates output tokens one after another, so more tokens take longer
Longer answers are always stored in Amazon S3 before being returned
The model re-reads its entire training data for every extra word
Output length has no effect on latency at all; only the length of the input prompt matters
notes: Correct. Generation is sequential: each new token depends on the ones before it, so total time grows with the number of output tokens.
Responses are streamed or returned directly; they are not saved to S3 first.
The model uses its learned weights; it never re-reads its training data during inference.
Both input and output length affect latency, and output length usually matters most.
questions.explain: LLMs generate text token by token, so response time grows with output length. Limiting maximum output tokens, asking for concise answers, and streaming responses all improve the user experience.

questions.q: What is an embedding?
options: A compressed ZIP file of a document stored in Amazon S3
A vector of numbers that represents the meaning of text, images, or other data
A short summary of each document, written by a human editor to make it easier to search
A filtering rule that blocks harmful or offensive words from appearing in model output
notes: Compression saves space but does not capture meaning.
Correct. An embedding model maps content to a vector so that items with similar meaning end up close together.
A human-written summary is text, not a numeric representation.
Blocking words is a guardrail feature, not an embedding.
questions.explain: Embeddings turn content into vectors in a high-dimensional space where distance reflects similarity of meaning. They power semantic search, RAG retrieval, recommendations, and clustering. Amazon Titan Text Embeddings is one embedding model available on Amazon Bedrock.

questions.q: A customer searches a help center for 'get my money back', and the top result is the article titled 'Refund policy', even though the words do not match. Which technique makes this possible?
options: Keyword matching that looks for the exact words of the query in each article's title
Semantic search that compares embeddings of the query and the articles
Sorting all of the help articles alphabetically by their title, then by publication date
Using a higher temperature for the search engine's results
notes: Exact keyword matching would miss this, because no words overlap.
Correct. Embeddings capture meaning, so 'money back' and 'refund' sit close together in vector space and the search finds the match.
Alphabetical order has nothing to do with relevance.
Temperature is a generation setting for FMs, not a search ranking method.
questions.explain: Semantic (vector) search embeds both the query and the documents, then returns the documents whose vectors are nearest to the query vector, for example by cosine similarity. This is the retrieval step behind RAG.

questions.q: Before loading 500-page manuals into a knowledge base, a team splits them into smaller passages. What is this step called, and why is it done?
options: Tokenization, so the manuals can be encrypted before they are stored in Amazon S3
Chunking, so retrieval returns focused passages that fit in the model's context
Fine-tuning, so the model memorizes every page of each manual
Distillation, so the manuals become smaller and cheaper to store in the knowledge base
notes: Tokenization splits text into tokens for the model; it is unrelated to encryption.
Correct. Chunking breaks documents into passages that are embedded separately, so the system can retrieve just the relevant parts.
Fine-tuning changes model weights; it is not how documents are prepared for retrieval.
Distillation trains a smaller model from a larger one; it does not shrink documents.
questions.explain: Chunking splits documents into pieces before they are embedded and stored in a vector database. Good chunks are small enough to be specific and to fit the context window, yet large enough to keep their meaning. Overlap between chunks helps preserve context.

questions.q: A RAG system uses very large chunks of about 8,000 tokens. Answers often include irrelevant details, and costs are high. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use smaller, more focused chunks, possibly with some overlap
Remove the vector database and send all documents in every prompt
Increase the chunk size further so each chunk holds more context
Set the temperature to 1.0 so the model chooses words more freely
notes: Correct. Smaller chunks make retrieval more precise and reduce the tokens passed to the model, which cuts noise and cost.
Sending every document in every prompt multiplies tokens and cost.
Even bigger chunks add more irrelevant text and cost.
Higher temperature adds randomness; it does not improve relevance.
questions.explain: Chunk size is a trade-off. Chunks that are too large dilute relevance and waste tokens. Chunks that are too small lose surrounding context. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases supports fixed-size, hierarchical, and semantic chunking to help balance this.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.1 (chunking); Bedrock Knowledge Bases chunking

questions.q: Which mechanism lets transformer-based LLMs weigh how strongly each word in a passage relates to every other word?
options: Recurrent loops that read text strictly one word at a time
Self-attention
Decision-tree splitting on word frequency
K-means clustering of sentences by length
notes: Recurrent networks read text sequentially; transformers replaced them largely because of attention.
Correct. Self-attention scores the relationships between all tokens in the input, which captures context and allows parallel processing.
Decision trees are a classic ML method, not how transformers model language.
Clustering groups data points; it is not part of the transformer architecture.
questions.explain: The transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, uses self-attention to model relationships between tokens regardless of their distance in the text. It is the basis of most modern LLMs and many multimodal models.

questions.q: How do diffusion models generate images?
options: By copying and stitching together pieces of existing images from their training data
By starting from random noise and removing noise step by step until an image emerges
By predicting the next word in a caption and drawing each word as it is written
By clustering pixels into groups and recoloring each group to match the prompt
notes: Diffusion models learn patterns; they do not retrieve and stitch training images.
Correct. During training the model learns to reverse a noising process; at generation time it denoises random noise into a new image guided by the prompt.
Next-token prediction describes LLMs, not image diffusion.
Pixel clustering is an image-processing technique, not generative diffusion.
questions.explain: Diffusion models power many text-to-image systems, such as Amazon Nova Canvas and Stable Diffusion. They learn to reverse a gradual noising process and are steered toward a prompt during denoising.

questions.q: An insurer wants customers to upload a photo of car damage, add a short description, and get back a written damage summary. What kind of model handles both the image and the text input?
options: A text-only language model
A multimodal model
A regression model
A speech-to-text model
notes: A text-only model cannot interpret the photo.
Correct. Multimodal models accept and reason over more than one type of input, such as images and text together.
Regression predicts a number from structured features.
Speech-to-text converts audio and cannot interpret photos.
