questions.explain: Multimodal foundation models process several modalities (text, images, sometimes audio or video) in one model. Several models on Amazon Bedrock, such as Amazon Nova Lite and Pro, accept image input.

questions.q: What makes a model a foundation model (FM)?
options: It is trained on one small labeled dataset to do one specific task as accurately as possible
It is pretrained on very broad data and can be adapted to many different tasks
It can only be used for image classification on a fixed set of labels
It is a rules engine written by domain experts without any training
notes: A narrow model trained for one task is the opposite of a foundation model.
Correct. FMs are large models pretrained on vast, broad datasets that serve as a base for many tasks through prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning.
FMs are general-purpose; they are not limited to one task.
FMs are learned from data, not hand-written rules.
questions.explain: Foundation models, such as LLMs and multimodal models, are pretrained once at great expense and then reused for many tasks. That reuse is what makes generative AI accessible to most companies.

questions.q: Put these stages of the foundation model lifecycle in order.
options: Select and prepare training data
Pretrain the model on the broad dataset
Fine-tune the model for specific tasks
Evaluate the model against benchmarks and requirements
Deploy the model and collect feedback
questions.explain: The FM lifecycle in the exam guide is: data selection, model selection, pretraining, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, and feedback. Feedback from production then informs the next round of improvement.

questions.q: Which tasks are good fits for generative AI? Select TWO.
options: Drafting first versions of marketing copy for review
Suggesting code completions to developers in their IDE
Calculating exact interest on a loan using a fixed formula
Controlling a car's emergency braking in real time
Reconciling ledger balances that must match to the cent
notes: Correct. Content drafts that people review are a classic GenAI use case.
Correct. Code generation and completion, as in Amazon Q Developer or Kiro, is a major GenAI use case.
Exact formula calculations need deterministic code, not a probabilistic model.
Safety-critical, millisecond control loops are not suited to generative models.
Exact reconciliation must be deterministic and auditable.
questions.explain: Generative AI excels at creating and transforming content: text, code, images, summaries, translations, and conversational assistants. It is a poor fit where exact, deterministic, or safety-critical outputs are needed.

questions.q: What does 'context engineering' mean for a foundation model application?
options: Designing the physical data center, cooling, and network where the model is hosted and served
Choosing what goes into the model's context window (instructions, retrieved data, tool results, memory) to get good results within token limits
Training a brand-new model from scratch using only the company's own documents and data
Encrypting the model's weights with AWS KMS before deploying the model to production
notes: Data center design is infrastructure work, not context engineering.
Correct. Context engineering curates everything the model sees for a given call: system instructions, relevant retrieved content, conversation history, memory, and tool outputs.
Training from scratch changes the model itself; context engineering works with an existing model.
Encrypting weights is a security control, not context design.
questions.explain: Version 1.1 adds context engineering (skill 2.1.5). It goes beyond writing one good prompt: it manages the whole context so the model gets the most relevant information without exceeding the context window or wasting tokens.

questions.q: A long-running support agent starts forgetting earlier instructions and giving worse answers as conversations grow past the model's context window. Which context engineering approach helps most?
options: Paste the entire conversation history and all product manuals into every single request to the model
Summarize older turns, keep key facts in memory, and retrieve only documents relevant to the current question
Switch to a model with a smaller context window to force shorter conversations
Raise the temperature so the model explores more options and is less likely to repeat itself
notes: Sending everything overflows the window, raises cost, and buries the important parts.
Correct. Compacting history, storing durable facts in memory, and retrieving selectively keep the context focused and within limits.
A smaller window makes the problem worse.
Temperature adds randomness; it does not restore lost context.
questions.explain: Good context engineering keeps the most relevant information in the window: concise system instructions, summaries of old turns, long-term memory for durable facts, and targeted retrieval. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory provides short-term and long-term memory for agents.

questions.q: What is a model's context window?
options: The maximum amount of text, in tokens, the model can consider in one request
The time window in which a model is available to receive API calls
The date range of the data the model was trained on, also known as its knowledge cutoff
The browser window in which a chatbot conversation is displayed
notes: Correct. The context window is the model's working memory for one call; it covers the prompt and, for most models, the generated output too.
Availability is an operational concern, not the context window.
That is the training data cutoff, a different concept.
The chat interface has nothing to do with the model's context window.
questions.explain: Context window size limits how much instruction, history, and retrieved content you can include. Larger windows allow more context but cost more tokens per request, which is why RAG and summarization are still useful.

questions.q: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
options: An AWS billing model that charges a fixed price for each model context opened by an application
An open standard that lets AI applications connect to external tools and data through a common client-server interface
A compression algorithm that shrinks long prompts before they are sent to a foundation model API
A proprietary file format, controlled by one vendor, for storing and sharing trained model weights
notes: MCP has nothing to do with billing.
Correct. MCP defines how an AI application (the client) discovers and calls tools, resources, and prompts exposed by MCP servers, so one integration works across many agents and models.
MCP does not compress prompts.
Model weight formats are a separate topic.
questions.explain: MCP is an open protocol introduced in late 2024 and now widely adopted. Instead of writing a custom integration for every tool and every agent framework, you expose a system once as an MCP server. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway can turn existing APIs and AWS Lambda functions into MCP-compatible tools.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.6 (MCP, new in v1.1)

questions.q: A company has three agent projects built with different frameworks. All of them need to read and update its internal ticketing system. What is the most reusable way to provide this access?
options: Write a separate custom integration for the ticketing system inside each agent's own code base
Expose the ticketing system once as an MCP server that every agent can call as a tool
Copy the entire ticket database into each agent's system prompt so the agents can read it directly
Fine-tune each agent's model on a snapshot of the tickets
notes: Separate integrations triple the work and drift apart over time.
Correct. An MCP server gives a standard tool interface that any MCP-compatible agent or framework can use.
Pasting a database into prompts is costly, stale, and cannot perform updates.
Fine-tuning bakes in a stale snapshot and cannot perform live updates.
questions.explain: MCP's value is reuse and standardization: build the tool integration once, and agents built with Strands Agents, LangGraph, or other frameworks can all call it.

questions.q: An agent needs today's exchange rate to answer a question. The model replies with a structured request to call a 'get_rate' function, the application runs the function, and the result is sent back to the model. What is this capability called?
options: Tool use (function calling)
Model distillation
Continued pretraining
Negative prompting
notes: Correct. With tool use, the model decides when to call a defined tool and with which arguments; the application executes it and returns the result.
Distillation trains a smaller model from a larger one.
Continued pretraining further trains a model on unlabeled data.
Negative prompting tells a model what to avoid in its output.
questions.explain: Tool use lets FMs reach live data and take actions: look up records, call APIs, run code. It is a core building block of agents. In Amazon Bedrock, the Converse API supports tool definitions across models.

questions.q: A travel assistant should remember each customer's seat preference and loyalty number across separate conversations weeks apart. Which agent capability is needed?
options: A higher temperature setting
Long-term memory
A larger embedding dimension
Short-term conversation memory only
notes: Temperature controls randomness, not recall of facts.
Correct. Long-term memory persists facts and preferences across sessions so the agent can use them later.
Embedding size affects retrieval quality, not whether facts persist across sessions.
Short-term memory lasts only within a session, so it would be lost between conversations.
questions.explain: Agents use short-term memory for the current session and long-term memory for durable facts, preferences, and summaries across sessions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory offers both as a managed capability.

questions.q: A customer service system uses one agent that reads each request and hands it to a billing agent, a technical support agent, or a returns agent, then combines their results. Which multi-agent pattern is this?
options: Supervisor (orchestrator and worker) pattern
Single-agent pattern with no delegation to other agents
Model distillation pattern
Batch inference pattern run on a nightly schedule
notes: Correct. A supervisor agent routes subtasks to specialized worker agents and assembles the final answer.
The scenario explicitly delegates to several agents.
Distillation is a training technique, not an agent pattern.
Batch inference is about offline bulk scoring.
questions.explain: Common multi-agent patterns include supervisor/orchestrator (one agent delegates to specialists), sequential pipelines, graphs, and swarms of peer agents. Specialized agents with focused tools and instructions are often more reliable than one agent doing everything.

questions.q: Match each agentic AI concept to its description.
prompts: The model calls an external API or function to get data or take an action
The agent keeps facts and preferences available across sessions
A standard way to expose tools and data to any compatible AI application
One agent delegates subtasks to specialized agents and combines results
Steps run in a defined sequence with branches, rather than being chosen freely by the model
options: Tool use
Long-term memory
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
Supervisor multi-agent pattern
Workflow orchestration
questions.explain: These are the agentic building blocks named in skill 2.1.6. Workflow orchestration suits predictable processes; autonomous agents suit open-ended tasks. Many real systems combine both.

questions.q: An insurance claims process must always follow the same steps: validate the form, check the policy, run fraud scoring, then route to approval. Auditors need the path to be predictable. Which design fits best?
options: A fully autonomous agent that decides its own steps on every claim
Workflow orchestration with defined steps, using AI models within individual steps
A single prompt asking an LLM to process the whole claim at once
A swarm of peer agents that negotiate among themselves the order of the steps for each claim
notes: Free-form agents may vary their path between claims, which hurts predictability and auditability.
Correct. An orchestrated workflow fixes the sequence and still uses AI where it helps, such as extracting fields or scoring fraud.
One prompt gives no control over, or audit trail of, each step.
Negotiated ordering is the least predictable option.
questions.explain: Use workflow orchestration (for example, Amazon Bedrock Flows or AWS Step Functions) when the process is known and must be repeatable. Use autonomous agents when the path cannot be known in advance.

questions.q: What is prompt engineering?
options: Designing and refining the instructions and context given to a model to get better outputs
Rewriting the model's source code and layers to change how its neural network architecture works
Building the GPUs and servers that the model runs on
Labeling training data with the correct answers for a supervised learning model to learn from
notes: Correct. Prompt engineering improves results by changing what you ask and how: instructions, context, examples, and output format.
Changing architecture is model development, not prompting.
Hardware is infrastructure, not prompting.
Labeling data prepares supervised training sets.
questions.explain: Prompt engineering is the cheapest way to improve FM output: no training, no new infrastructure. Techniques include clear instructions, role and context, few-shot examples, chain-of-thought, and output format specification.

questions.q: At a basic level, how does an LLM generate a response?
options: It looks up the exact answer in a database of verified facts and returns that answer
It repeatedly predicts the most likely next token given everything so far
It runs a search engine query and returns the first result word for word
It selects a pre-written answer from a fixed list of templates
notes: LLMs do not query a fact database (unless you add retrieval); this is also why they can hallucinate.
Correct. LLMs generate text one token at a time by sampling from a probability distribution over possible next tokens.
LLMs do not run web searches by default.
LLMs generate new text rather than picking fixed templates.
questions.explain: Next-token prediction explains both the strengths of LLMs (fluent, flexible text) and their weaknesses (they can produce plausible but false statements, and outputs vary between runs).

questions.q: A team needs to convert 1 million product descriptions into vectors for semantic search. What type of model should it use?
options: A text-to-image diffusion model that generates a picture for each description
An embedding model, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings
A speech synthesis model such as Amazon Polly
A large chat model with temperature set to zero
notes: Diffusion models generate images; they do not produce vectors for search.
Correct. Embedding models output numeric vectors that represent meaning, ready for storage in a vector database.
Polly produces audio, not vectors.
Chat models generate text; producing vectors is the job of an embedding model.
questions.explain: Generation models create content; embedding models create vector representations. RAG systems use both: an embedding model for indexing and retrieval, and a generation model for the final answer.

questions.q: A marketing team wants to create dozens of new product images in different styles from text descriptions. Which kind of model fits?
options: An image generation model such as Amazon Nova Canvas
A text classification model trained on product categories
A time-series forecasting model fed with historical sales
An embedding model that turns product text into vectors
notes: Correct. Text-to-image models generate new images from prompts; Amazon Nova Canvas is Amazon's image generation model on Bedrock.
Classification assigns labels; it does not create images.
Forecasting predicts future values from history.
Embedding models create vectors, not images.
questions.explain: Image, video, and audio generation are listed GenAI use cases. Amazon Nova includes Nova Canvas for images and Nova Reel for video.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.2; Amazon Nova overview

questions.q: The same 1,000-word document costs noticeably different amounts to process with two different models on Amazon Bedrock. What best explains this?
options: Amazon Bedrock charges a fixed fee per document, regardless of the model
Models use different tokenizers and per-token prices, so token count and rate both vary
The second model must be quietly adding hidden words to the document before processing it
On-demand cost depends only on the time of day the request is made, not on the model chosen
notes: On-demand Bedrock pricing is per token, not per document.
Correct. Each model family splits text into tokens differently, and each has its own input and output price per token.
Models do not add hidden words; tokenization simply differs.
On-demand pricing does not depend on the time of day.
questions.explain: Token counts for the same text vary by tokenizer, and prices vary by model size and provider. Compare models on both quality and the real cost of your typical prompts.

questions.q: What is the role of a vector database in a generative AI application?
options: It stores embeddings and quickly finds the ones nearest to a query vector
It trains the foundation model on new documents every night
It stores the model's weights so the model can run without a GPU
It replaces the foundation model entirely by storing every possible answer
notes: Correct. Vector stores index embeddings for fast similarity (nearest-neighbor) search, the retrieval step in RAG.
Vector databases do not train models.
Model weights are not served from a vector database.
A vector store retrieves context; the FM still writes the answer.
questions.explain: On AWS, vector storage options include Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL and Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL with pgvector, and Amazon Neptune. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases can manage the vector store for you.

questions.q: An application sends 500 input tokens and receives 2,000 output tokens per request. The model charges 5 times more per output token than per input token. Which change will reduce cost the most?
options: Ask for shorter answers and set a lower maximum output token limit
Shorten the 500-token prompt to 400 tokens
Move the application to a larger model in the same family
Turn on prompt caching for the 500-token prompt
notes: Correct. Output tokens dominate this bill (2,000 tokens at 5 times the price), so trimming output saves the most.
Saving 100 input tokens is small next to 2,000 expensive output tokens.
Larger models usually cost more per token.
Caching helps when a long shared prefix repeats. Here the input is short and output is the main cost.
questions.explain: Token-based pricing charges input and output tokens separately, and output tokens usually cost more. Look at where the tokens are before optimizing. Output length also drives latency, because tokens are generated one at a time.

questions.q: An agent calls a search tool that returns about 30,000 tokens of raw web pages for every query. The agent becomes slow and expensive, and its answers drift off-topic. Which context engineering practice helps most?
options: Trim or summarize tool results so only the relevant parts enter the context
Raise the model's temperature to handle the extra text
Append every tool result from every earlier turn to each new prompt
Switch off the system prompt to make room for the search results
notes: Correct. Context engineering selects and compresses what enters the window, including tool outputs.
Temperature affects randomness, not how much irrelevant text the model must read.
Accumulating every tool result makes the context even larger and noisier.
The system prompt carries essential instructions. Removing it makes behavior worse.
questions.explain: Context engineering (skill 2.1.5) manages everything in the window: instructions, retrieved documents, tool results, conversation history, and memory. More context is not always better: irrelevant tokens add cost, latency, and distraction.

questions.q: A company's travel agent, built with one framework, must hand off a task to a partner's hotel-booking agent, built by another team with a different framework, and get the result back. Which open standard is designed for this agent-to-agent communication?
options: The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol
The Model Context Protocol (MCP)
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
notes: Correct. A2A is an open protocol for agents to discover each other, exchange tasks, and return results across frameworks and vendors.
MCP connects an agent to tools and data sources. It is not designed for one autonomous agent to delegate to another.
Prompt Management stores and versions prompts. It does not connect agents.
RAG retrieves documents for a model. It is not an agent communication standard.
questions.explain: Multi-agent communication patterns are part of skill 2.1.6. Remember the split: MCP connects agents to tools and data; A2A connects agents to other agents. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime supports both.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.6; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore docs

questions.q: Match each multi-agent pattern to its description.
prompts: One agent receives the request, delegates subtasks to specialist agents, and combines their results
Agents run in a fixed order, each passing its output to the next
Peer agents share a task and hand off to whichever agent is best suited, with no central controller
Agents are connected as nodes with defined edges and conditions that decide the next step
options: Supervisor (orchestrator-worker)
Sequential pipeline
Swarm
Graph
Single agent
questions.explain: Skill 2.1.6 covers multi-agent system patterns. Supervisor patterns centralize control, sequential pipelines suit fixed processes, swarms let peers collaborate, and graphs give explicit, conditional control flow. Strands Agents supports these patterns.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.6; Strands Agents docs

questions.q: A shopping agent needs to remember what the customer said three messages ago in the current chat, and also the customer's shoe size from a conversation last month. Which memory design fits?
options: Short-term memory for the current session and long-term memory for durable facts across sessions
Long-term memory only, storing every token of every conversation permanently for all users
No memory at all, relying on the model's pretraining knowledge to recall customer details
A larger context window only, with nothing stored between separate conversations
notes: Correct. Short-term memory keeps the current conversation; long-term memory extracts and keeps lasting facts and preferences.
Storing every token forever is costly and noisy. Long-term memory should keep extracted, useful facts.
Pretraining knowledge does not include this customer's details.
A context window holds only the current request. Without stored memory, last month's shoe size is gone.
questions.explain: Memory management is part of skill 2.1.6. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory provides both short-term memory (session events) and long-term memory (extracted facts, preferences, and summaries).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.1.6; AgentCore Memory docs

questions.q: Which statements about tokens and embeddings are correct? Select TWO.
options: An embedding is a numeric vector that captures the meaning of content
Texts with similar meaning tend to have embeddings that are close together
A token is always exactly one complete English word
Embeddings are used only for image generation
Chunking means converting text into tokens
notes: Correct. Embedding models map text, images, or other data to vectors.
Correct. Distance between vectors reflects semantic similarity, which powers semantic search.
Tokens are often parts of words, and punctuation can be its own token.
Embeddings power search, RAG, recommendations, and clustering.
Chunking splits documents into passages. Tokenization converts text into tokens.
questions.explain: Skill 2.1.1 defines tokens, chunking, embeddings, and vectors. Don't mix up tokenization (text to tokens), chunking (documents to passages), and embedding (content to vectors).

questions.q: A lawyer asks an LLM for case law. The model confidently cites a court case, with a name and year, that does not exist. What is this called?
options: Hallucination
Overfitting during training
Prompt caching
Model drift after deployment over several months
notes: Correct. A hallucination is fluent, plausible output that is false or not supported by any source.
Overfitting describes a model that memorizes training data and generalizes poorly; it is not the term for invented facts.
Prompt caching reuses repeated prompt prefixes to save cost.
Drift is gradual change in data or performance over time, not a single invented fact.
questions.explain: LLMs predict likely text, not verified truth, so they can invent facts, citations, and numbers. Mitigations include grounding answers with RAG, asking for citations, contextual grounding checks in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and human review for high-stakes use.

questions.q: A team notices that sending the exact same prompt to its model twice often gives two differently worded answers. Which limitation of generative AI is this, and what reduces it?
options: Nondeterminism; lowering the temperature makes outputs more consistent
Hallucination; raising the temperature makes outputs more factual
Bias; adding more GPUs to the endpoint makes outputs fairer
Overfitting; training the model for more epochs makes outputs repeatable
notes: Correct. Generation samples from probabilities, so outputs vary. Lower temperature (and top-p) makes the model pick the most likely tokens more often.
Different wording is not the same as false content, and higher temperature increases variation.
Bias concerns unfair outcomes, and GPU count does not affect it.
Training more epochs does not make sampling deterministic and can cause overfitting.
questions.explain: Nondeterminism is a listed GenAI disadvantage. It matters for testing, auditing, and consistency. Lower temperature, fixed output formats, and validation of outputs reduce its impact.

questions.q: A compliance officer asks exactly why an LLM recommended one insurance plan over another. The team cannot trace the decision to specific inputs. Which limitation does this show?
options: Poor interpretability
Low throughput under heavy load
Insufficient context window size for long documents
High training data quality
notes: Correct. Large neural models with billions of parameters are hard to interpret; it is difficult to say why a specific output was produced.
Throughput concerns speed, not explaining decisions.
Context size limits input length; it does not explain why the decision cannot be traced.
High data quality would be an advantage, not a limitation.
questions.explain: Interpretability is a key GenAI disadvantage, and it drives the v1.1 objective about choosing traditional ML when explainability is required. Documenting models (SageMaker Model Cards) and evaluating outputs help, but they do not make an LLM fully transparent.

questions.q: A company uses one foundation model to summarize reports, translate emails, draft product descriptions, and answer HR questions, without training a separate model for each. Which advantage of generative AI does this show?
options: Adaptability
Determinism
Low interpretability
Perfect factual accuracy on every topic
notes: Correct. One FM can adapt to many tasks through prompting, which is a major advantage.
GenAI outputs are not deterministic.
Low interpretability is a disadvantage, not an advantage.
FMs can make mistakes and hallucinate; accuracy is not guaranteed.
questions.explain: The v1.1 guide lists adaptability, responsiveness, conversational capabilities, and the ability to generate content as GenAI advantages.

questions.q: An airline replaces its menu-based phone system with an assistant that understands free-form questions and replies naturally, 24 hours a day. Which GenAI advantage is most evident?
options: Conversational capabilities and responsiveness
Guaranteed deterministic outputs for audits
Easier explanation of every decision to regulators
Zero risk of incorrect answers
notes: Correct. FMs hold natural, flexible conversations and respond instantly at any hour.
GenAI outputs vary; determinism is not a strength.
Explaining decisions is a weakness of large models.
GenAI can be wrong; risk must be managed, not assumed away.
questions.explain: Conversational ability and responsiveness are why GenAI is popular for customer service. The trade-off is managing hallucinations and inconsistency, for example with guardrails, RAG, and human handoff.

questions.q: Which of these are disadvantages of generative AI that a business must plan for? Select TWO.
options: Hallucinations
Nondeterministic outputs
Adaptability across many tasks
Natural conversational ability
The ability to generate new content
notes: Correct. Models can produce confident but false statements.
Correct. The same input can give different outputs, which complicates testing and consistency.
Adaptability is an advantage.
Conversational ability is an advantage.
Content generation is an advantage.
questions.explain: The guide's GenAI disadvantages are hallucinations, poor interpretability, inaccuracy, and nondeterminism. Its advantages are adaptability, responsiveness, conversational capabilities, and content generation.

questions.q: A voice assistant must start answering within a fraction of a second. Answers are short and simple. Which model choice fits best?
options: A smaller, faster model that meets the quality bar for the task
The largest available model, regardless of how long it takes to respond
A model with the biggest context window, even if it is slow
An image generation model tuned for photorealism
notes: Correct. For latency-critical, simple tasks, a smaller model is usually faster and cheaper while still good enough.
The largest models are typically slower and more expensive; size is not the goal in itself.
A big context window is not needed for short answers and can add latency and cost.
Image generation models do not produce spoken answers.
questions.explain: Model selection weighs model type, performance, capabilities, constraints, compliance, cost, latency, and complexity (v1.1 adds cost, latency, and complexity). Pick the smallest model that meets the requirement.

questions.q: A European bank must keep all customer data processed by its AI assistant inside the EU. Which model selection factor is most important here?
options: Compliance, including the Regions where the model is available
The number of languages the model's marketing site supports
How many parameters the model has
Whether the model can generate images
notes: Correct. Regulatory requirements limit which models and Regions can be used. Check that the model is offered in an EU Region and how any cross-Region inference is configured.
Marketing language support is irrelevant to data residency.
Parameter count does not determine where data is processed.
Image generation is not a requirement in this scenario.
questions.explain: Compliance constraints such as data residency, industry regulations, and licensing often rule models in or out before quality is even compared. In Amazon Bedrock, model availability varies by Region.

questions.q: A company must classify 50 million short customer messages a month into five categories. A small model already achieves the needed accuracy in tests. What is the best choice?
options: Use the small model, because it meets the requirement at much lower cost and latency
Use the largest model available, because bigger always means better business value
Fine-tune the largest available model on all historical messages before testing anything else
Avoid AI and have people read all 50 million messages
notes: Correct. When a smaller model is good enough, it wins on cost, speed, and simplicity, which matters a lot at this volume.
Bigger models cost more per token; the extra capability is wasted on a simple task.
Fine-tuning a large model adds cost and effort, and it is unnecessary when a small model already meets the bar.
Manual review of 50 million messages a month is impractical.
questions.explain: Right-size the model: match capability to the task's complexity, then optimize for cost and latency. At high volume, small differences in per-token price add up to large differences in total cost.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.2.3 (cost, latency, model complexity)

questions.q: A field-service app needs a model that can look at a photo of a broken machine part and describe the fault in words. Which selection factor rules out many models?
options: Model capabilities, specifically multimodal image input
The model's knowledge cutoff date for current events
Whether the model supports streaming text output
The maximum output length allowed per request
notes: Correct. Only models that accept image input (multimodal models) can do this task at all.
Knowledge cutoff matters for current events, not for describing a photo.
Streaming affects how output is delivered, not whether the model can see images.
Output length is not the deciding factor here.
questions.explain: Start model selection with hard requirements: modality (text, image, audio), context length, languages, and compliance. Then compare quality, cost, and latency among the models that qualify.

questions.q: An online store uses generative AI to write better product descriptions. Which business metric best shows whether the descriptions help sales?
options: Conversion rate
Training loss
Token count per description
Model parameter count
notes: Correct. Conversion rate, the share of visitors who buy, directly reflects whether better descriptions lead to purchases.
Training loss is a technical metric used while training models.
Token count measures length and cost, not sales impact.
Parameter count describes the model, not business results.
questions.explain: Tie GenAI projects to business outcomes. Typical metrics are conversion rate, average revenue per user (ARPU), customer lifetime value (CLV), efficiency, accuracy, and ROI.

questions.q: What does ARPU measure?
options: Average revenue per user over a period
Accuracy rate per uploaded file
Annual requests per unit of compute
Average response time per user query
notes: Correct. ARPU = total revenue / number of users for a period. GenAI features such as personalization aim to raise it.
This is not a standard business metric.
This is not what ARPU stands for.
Response time is a latency metric, not ARPU.
questions.explain: Average revenue per user is a common way to judge whether AI-driven features, such as recommendations or upsell assistants, increase how much each customer spends.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.2.4 (average revenue per user)

questions.q: A subscription service adds AI-personalized recommendations to keep customers engaged and subscribed for longer. Which metric best captures this long-term goal?
options: Customer lifetime value (CLV)
Words generated per minute
Embedding dimension of the recommender
Number of prompts tested in development
notes: Correct. CLV estimates the total revenue a customer brings over the whole relationship, so it rises when customers stay longer.
Generation speed is a technical measure, not a business outcome.
Embedding dimension is an implementation detail.
Prompts tested is a development activity measure.
questions.explain: CLV is the right metric when the goal is retention and long-term value rather than one-off conversions.

questions.q: After deploying a GenAI tool that drafts replies, support agents close 35% more tickets per hour. Which type of business value does this show?
options: Efficiency (productivity)
Model accuracy on a benchmark
Lower model latency
Higher model temperature
notes: Correct. More output per hour of human work is an efficiency gain.
Benchmark accuracy is a model metric, not observed business value.
Latency is a technical property of the model.
Temperature is a generation setting.
questions.explain: Efficiency gains, meaning time saved or output per employee, are among the most common and measurable benefits of GenAI.

questions.q: Match each business goal to the metric that measures it best.
prompts: More website visitors complete a purchase
Each customer spends more per month
Customers stay subscribed for more years
The project's gains exceed what it cost to build and run
options: Conversion rate
Average revenue per user (ARPU)
Customer lifetime value (CLV)
Return on investment (ROI)
questions.explain: Conversion rate tracks purchases per visit, ARPU tracks revenue per user per period, CLV tracks revenue over the whole relationship, and ROI compares benefit with total cost.

questions.q: A law firm wants a public FAQ assistant that answers questions about its services. A wrong answer could create legal risk. Which approach best manages the hallucination risk?
options: Ground answers in approved documents with RAG, require citations, and route sensitive questions to a human
Use the largest model available, trust its answers without checks, and publish every reply immediately
Raise the temperature so the model gives more varied answers
Remove all instructions from the system prompt so the model answers freely in whatever style it prefers
notes: Correct. Grounding plus citations reduces invented answers, and human escalation covers high-risk cases.
No model is hallucination-free; trusting it blindly is risky.
Higher temperature increases randomness and the chance of errors.
Removing instructions removes control and makes errors more likely.
questions.explain: GenAI's limits do not rule it out for sensitive uses, but they require controls: grounding (RAG), clear instructions, guardrails, output validation, and human-in-the-loop review where stakes are high.

questions.q: One foundation model performs well on legal summaries, marketing copy, and code explanations alike. Which business value term describes this strength?
options: Cross-domain performance
Low inference latency
Deterministic output
Small model size
notes: Correct. Strong results across many domains means one model can serve many teams, which increases its business value.
Latency is a separate property and is not described here.
GenAI outputs are not deterministic.
Strong cross-domain models are often large, not small.
questions.explain: The guide lists cross-domain performance among GenAI business value factors: a model that handles many domains reduces the number of separate solutions to build and maintain.

questions.q: A startup is choosing a model for a mobile app that answers short questions. It has a tight budget, and users expect near-instant replies. Which selection factors matter most? Select TWO.
options: Cost per token
Latency
Image generation quality
Maximum supported video length
Ability to write long novels
notes: Correct. A tight budget makes per-token cost a key factor.
Correct. Near-instant replies make latency a key factor.
The app does not generate images.
The app does not process video.
Long-form creative writing is not required here.
questions.explain: Let the requirements drive selection. For short, frequent answers, cost and latency usually dominate. Capabilities the app will never use should not drive the choice.

questions.q: A company must choose a model for a narrow, high-volume classification task. The largest model is only 1% more accurate than a much smaller one but costs 15 times more and is 4 times slower. Which selection factor should drive the decision?
options: Model complexity relative to the task, weighed against cost and latency
Always the highest benchmark accuracy, whatever the cost
The size of each model's marketing website
Whether the model can also generate images
notes: Correct. v1.1 adds cost, latency, and model complexity to the selection factors. A simpler model that meets the bar is usually the better business choice.
Maximizing accuracy alone ignores cost and latency, which also matter to the business.
Marketing material is not a selection factor.
Image generation is irrelevant to a text classification task.
questions.explain: Right-size the model: complex models are worth it only when the task needs them. For simple, high-volume tasks, smaller models usually give the best business value.

questions.q: A GenAI assistant usually answers correctly but sometimes gives slightly wrong figures when it summarizes financial reports. Which disadvantage of generative AI is this?
options: Inaccuracy
Adaptability
Responsiveness
Conversational capability
notes: Correct. Inaccuracy, along with hallucinations, interpretability, and nondeterminism, is a listed disadvantage of GenAI.
Adaptability is an advantage: one model handles many tasks.
Responsiveness is an advantage: fast, on-demand answers.
Conversational capability is an advantage of GenAI.
questions.explain: Know the lists: advantages are adaptability, responsiveness, conversational capabilities, and the ability to generate content; disadvantages are hallucinations, interpretability, inaccuracy, and nondeterminism. For figures, validate outputs against the source data.

questions.q: An e-commerce company wants to prove that its new GenAI shopping assistant creates business value. Which metrics measure business value rather than model quality? Select TWO.
options: Conversion rate of sessions that used the assistant
Change in average revenue per user (ARPU)
BERTScore of the assistant's answers
Perplexity on a held-out text set
ROUGE-L compared with reference answers
notes: Correct. Conversion rate is a listed business metric for GenAI.
Correct. ARPU shows whether the assistant increases spend per user.
BERTScore measures semantic similarity of text, a model quality metric.
Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text, not business outcomes.
ROUGE-L measures text overlap, not business value.
questions.explain: Skill 2.2.4 lists cross-domain performance, ROI, efficiency, conversion rate, ARPU, accuracy, and customer lifetime value. Pair model metrics with business metrics to justify investment.

questions.q: Which AWS service offers foundation models from Amazon and other leading AI companies through a single API, as a fully managed, serverless service?
options: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon EC2 with GPU instances that you configure and patch yourself
Amazon Comprehend
AWS Glue
notes: Correct. Amazon Bedrock gives API access to many FMs (including Amazon Nova and models from providers such as Anthropic, Meta, and Mistral) with no infrastructure to manage.
EC2 can host models, but you manage the servers, scaling, and model serving yourself.
Comprehend is a task-specific NLP service, not a catalog of FMs.
Glue is a data integration and ETL service.
questions.explain: Amazon Bedrock is the core managed GenAI service on AWS. Alongside model access it provides Knowledge Bases (RAG), Guardrails, Agents, Flows, Prompt Management, model evaluation, and model customization.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.1; Amazon Bedrock overview

questions.q: A team wants to deploy an open-weight foundation model to its own endpoint with a few clicks, then fine-tune it on company data. It is comfortable managing an endpoint. Which option is designed for this?
options: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
notes: Correct. JumpStart deploys open-weight FMs to SageMaker AI endpoints you control and supports fine-tuning them.
Bedrock on-demand is serverless: you call an API and never run or size your own endpoint.
Canvas is a no-code ML tool for analysts, not the place to deploy and manage an open-weight FM endpoint.
Knowledge Bases adds RAG over your documents. It does not deploy or fine-tune a model.
questions.explain: JumpStart sits inside SageMaker AI. It trades some convenience for control: you choose the instance type and run the endpoint, unlike the serverless Amazon Bedrock API.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.1 (SageMaker JumpStart, added in v1.1)

questions.q: A company wants to add a generative AI chat feature with the least operational overhead. It has no ML engineers and does not want to manage servers. Which option fits best?
options: Call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock
Train a custom LLM on Amazon EC2 GPU instances
Host an open-source model on a self-managed Amazon EKS cluster
Build a model from scratch in SageMaker AI notebooks
notes: Correct. Bedrock is serverless: you call an API and AWS runs the models.
Training a custom LLM needs ML expertise, data, and large GPU budgets.
Running models on EKS means managing clusters, scaling, and model serving.
Building from scratch is the highest-effort option.
questions.explain: 'Least operational overhead' usually points to the most managed service. For FM access that is Amazon Bedrock. Choose SageMaker AI when you need more control over models, training, or infrastructure.

questions.q: A developer wants to build an AI agent in Python with a few lines of code: give it a model, a prompt, and some tools, and let the model plan which tools to call. Which open-source SDK from AWS is built for this?
options: Strands Agents
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
Kiro
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
notes: Correct. Strands Agents is an open-source, model-driven SDK: define a model, a prompt, and tools, and the model plans the steps.
AgentCore Runtime hosts agents in production. You still need a framework, such as Strands, to write the agent.
Kiro is an IDE that helps developers write code. It is not an SDK that the agent itself is built with.
Prompt Management stores and versions prompts. It does not run an agent loop or call tools.
questions.explain: Strands Agents, new in v1.1, lets the model's reasoning drive the agent loop instead of hard-coded workflows. Agents built with it can run anywhere, including on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.1 (Strands Agents, new in v1.1)

questions.q: A company has built agents with several frameworks. It now needs secure, scalable hosting for them with session isolation, memory, identity controls, tool gateways, and observability, without managing infrastructure. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Strands Agents
Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
notes: Correct. AgentCore provides Runtime, Memory, Gateway, Identity, Observability, and Policy for agents built with any framework.
Strands Agents is a framework for writing agents. It does not provide managed hosting, identity, or observability.
Knowledge Bases provides managed RAG. It does not host agents or manage their identities.
JumpStart deploys and fine-tunes models on SageMaker AI endpoints. It is not an agent hosting platform.
questions.explain: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, new in v1.1, is framework-agnostic (Strands Agents, LangGraph, CrewAI, and others) and model-agnostic. It handles the operational problems of running agents in production.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.1 (Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, new in v1.1)

questions.q: Match each Amazon Bedrock AgentCore capability to what it does.
prompts: Runs agents serverlessly with isolated sessions
Keeps short-term and long-term context for agents
Turns existing APIs and Lambda functions into tools agents can call
Manages how agents authenticate and what they may access
Traces and monitors agent behavior in production
options: AgentCore Runtime
AgentCore Memory
AgentCore Gateway
AgentCore Identity
AgentCore Observability
questions.explain: AgentCore is modular, so you can use one capability or several. Runtime hosts agents, Memory stores context, Gateway exposes tools (including as MCP tools), Identity handles agent authentication and authorization, and Observability provides tracing and dashboards. Policy in AgentCore adds controls over what actions agents can take.
questions.ref: Exam guide skills 2.3.1 and 5.1.1; Amazon Bedrock AgentCore docs

questions.q: A development team wants an agentic AI coding assistant that works in the IDE, turns a feature request into requirements and a task list, writes the code, and connects to the team's internal tools through MCP servers. Which AWS offering is designed for this?
options: Kiro
Strands Agents
Amazon Quick
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
notes: Correct. Kiro is AWS's agentic IDE: it uses spec-driven development (requirements, design, tasks), agent hooks, and MCP servers to help developers ship code.
Strands Agents is an open-source SDK for building your own agents in code. It is not a coding assistant for developers.
Amazon Quick is an agentic workspace for business users (dashboards, research, automation), not an IDE.
AgentCore Runtime hosts agents you have built in production. It does not help developers write code.
questions.explain: Know the v1.1 developer offerings apart: Kiro helps developers write software (agentic IDE and CLI); Strands Agents is an SDK to build agents; AgentCore runs agents in production; Amazon Quick serves business users. AWS has named Kiro the successor to the IDE features of Amazon Q Developer.

questions.q: A company wants to use agentic AI to speed up modernizing legacy mainframe and .NET applications for the cloud. Which AWS service is built for this?
options: AWS Transform
Kiro
Strands Agents
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
notes: Correct. AWS Transform uses specialized AI agents for large-scale modernization of mainframe, .NET, and VMware workloads.
Kiro helps developers write and change code in general. It is not a purpose-built migration and modernization service.
Strands Agents is an SDK for building your own agents, which would mean building a modernization tool yourself.
AgentCore runs agents you build. It does not itself modernize applications.
questions.explain: AWS Transform was added to the in-scope services in v1.1. It is an example of agentic AI applied to a specific, high-value enterprise task.
questions.ref: Exam guide in-scope services (AWS Transform, added in v1.1)

questions.q: What is Amazon Nova?
options: Amazon's own family of foundation models, available through Amazon Bedrock
A database service that stores vectors for similarity search
A security service that scans S3 buckets for personal data
A service that labels training data using a workforce of human annotators
notes: Correct. Amazon Nova includes understanding models (such as Nova Micro, Lite, and Pro) and creative models (such as Nova Canvas for images and Nova Reel for video).
Vector storage is provided by services such as OpenSearch Service or Aurora.
Scanning S3 for sensitive data is Amazon Macie.
Human labeling is SageMaker Ground Truth.
questions.explain: Nova models are built by Amazon and offered in Bedrock alongside third-party models. Smaller Nova models are positioned for low cost and latency; larger ones for complex reasoning.

questions.q: A startup ships a generative AI feature in three weeks using Amazon Bedrock instead of spending months standing up GPU infrastructure. Which advantage of AWS GenAI services does this show most directly?
options: Speed to market
Guaranteed hallucination-free answers
No responsibility for data security
Unlimited free usage
notes: Correct. Managed services remove infrastructure work, so teams deliver value much faster.
No service can guarantee hallucination-free output.
Under the shared responsibility model, customers still secure their data and access.
Bedrock is pay-as-you-go, not free.
questions.explain: The guide lists accessibility, a lower barrier to entry, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and speed to market as advantages of AWS GenAI services.

questions.q: A small business with no data scientists builds a useful document Q&A tool using Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Which advantage of AWS GenAI services does this best illustrate?
options: Lower barrier to entry
Higher model interpretability
Fully deterministic outputs
Free GPUs for every account
notes: Correct. Managed, pre-integrated capabilities let teams without ML expertise build GenAI applications.
Managed services do not make models more interpretable.
Outputs remain probabilistic.
GPUs are not free; managed services simply hide them.
questions.explain: Managed RAG, guardrails, and agents mean you do not need to assemble vector databases, embedding pipelines, and orchestration code yourself.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.2 (lower barrier to entry)

questions.q: A healthcare company worries that prompts containing patient information could be used to train the models it calls. What does Amazon Bedrock state about this?
options: Prompts and outputs are not used to train the base models or shared with model providers
Every prompt is shared with the model provider to improve future models
Prompts are stored publicly so the community can audit model quality
Data protection depends on each model provider, and Bedrock itself gives no assurances
notes: Correct. Bedrock does not use your prompts and completions to train AWS or third-party models, and does not share them with model providers.
Bedrock does not pass customer prompts to providers for training.
Customer data is never published.
Bedrock provides the same data protection across the models it hosts.
questions.explain: Bedrock also encrypts data in transit and at rest, keeps data in the Region you use (unless you opt into cross-Region inference), and supports private connectivity with AWS PrivateLink. Customers still control access with IAM.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.3; Amazon Bedrock data protection

questions.q: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task stays with the customer when using Amazon Bedrock?
options: Controlling which users and applications can invoke models, and protecting the data they send
Patching the operating systems of the servers that host the foundation models
Physically securing the data centers, power, and cooling systems that run Bedrock
Maintaining and upgrading the network hardware and cabling inside each AWS Region
notes: Correct. Customers are responsible for security in the cloud: IAM permissions, data classification, guardrails, and how outputs are used.
Server patching for a managed service is AWS's job.
Physical data center security is AWS's job.
AWS manages its own network hardware.
questions.explain: AWS secures the cloud itself (infrastructure and managed service operations). Customers secure what they put in and build on it: identities, data, application logic, and responsible use.
questions.ref: Exam guide skills 2.3.3 and 5.1.1 (shared responsibility model)

questions.q: A company's GenAI app has steady, high, predictable traffic and needs guaranteed throughput during business hours. Which Amazon Bedrock pricing option is designed for this?
options: Provisioned Throughput
On-demand pay-per-token with no reservation
Batch inference jobs submitted once a day
The AWS Free Tier
notes: Correct. Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model capacity (model units) for an hourly charge, which suits consistent, high-volume workloads.
On-demand is flexible and pay-per-use, but it does not guarantee capacity at high volume.
Batch inference is for offline jobs, not live traffic.
The Free Tier is not meant for production workloads.
questions.explain: Bedrock pricing trade-offs: on-demand (pay per token, no commitment), batch (lower price for non-urgent bulk jobs), and Provisioned Throughput (reserved capacity, billed hourly, optionally with a term commitment).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.4 (provisioned throughput); Amazon Bedrock pricing

questions.q: A company needs to summarize 2 million archived documents. Results are needed within a few days, not instantly. How can it cut cost on Amazon Bedrock?
options: Use batch inference, which is priced lower than on-demand for supported models
Buy Provisioned Throughput with a one-year commitment for the job
Send each document through on-demand calls as fast as possible, in parallel
Raise the temperature to finish each summary faster
notes: Correct. Bedrock batch inference processes large sets of prompts asynchronously at a discounted price (around 50% lower than on-demand for supported models).
A year of reserved capacity is costly for a one-off job.
On-demand works but costs more than batch for bulk, non-urgent work.
Temperature affects randomness, not speed or price.
questions.explain: Match pricing to responsiveness needs: real-time traffic uses on-demand or Provisioned Throughput, while large offline workloads use batch inference.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.4 (responsiveness trade-offs); Bedrock batch inference

questions.q: A team fine-tuned a model in Amazon Bedrock and bought Provisioned Throughput to serve it. On quiet days with almost no traffic, the bill is still high. What is the most likely reason?
options: Provisioned Throughput is billed for every hour the capacity is reserved, whether or not requests arrive
Fine-tuned models are charged again every day for each character of the training data used
Bedrock charges a daily fee for every prompt template saved in Prompt Management
Custom models are billed only by the number of failed requests they receive
notes: Correct. Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity at an hourly rate, so idle hours cost the same as busy ones.
Training is a one-time cost based on tokens processed, not a daily charge.
Saving prompt templates does not drive this kind of cost.
Billing is not based on failed requests.
questions.explain: Customization has two cost parts: training (one-time) and serving (ongoing). Some custom models can now be served on demand and billed per token, but others require Provisioned Throughput, which is billed hourly. Weigh prompt engineering and RAG first, and check the serving options for your model before you customize.
questions.ref: Exam guide skills 2.3.4 (custom models, provisioned throughput) and 3.1.5; Amazon Bedrock pricing

questions.q: An app hits throughput limits in one Region during traffic spikes. The team wants requests routed automatically to other Regions in the same geography. Which Amazon Bedrock feature helps, and what must they check?
options: Cross-Region inference; check that routing within the geography meets their data residency rules
Prompt caching; check that the cache is encrypted with a customer managed key
Batch inference; check the size of the output S3 bucket
Model distillation; check that the teacher model's license allows creating a smaller student model
notes: Correct. Cross-Region inference spreads requests across Regions in a geography for higher throughput and availability, but data may be processed outside the source Region.
Caching reduces repeated-prefix cost; it does not add Regional capacity.
Batch inference is for offline jobs, not live spikes.
Distillation creates a smaller model; it does not route traffic.
questions.explain: Regional coverage and availability are cost and design trade-offs. Cross-Region inference improves resilience to spikes but has data residency implications that compliance teams must review.

questions.q: A team deploys its self-hosted model endpoint in two Regions so the app keeps working if one Region has problems. What is the main trade-off?
options: Higher availability and redundancy, at a higher cost
Lower cost, but less availability
Better model accuracy, at the same cost
Fewer tokens per request, but higher latency for every user
notes: Correct. Redundant deployments improve resilience but roughly double the hosting cost.
Running in two Regions costs more, not less.
Redundancy does not change model accuracy.
Deployment topology does not change token counts.
questions.explain: The guide asks you to weigh responsiveness, availability, redundancy, performance, and regional coverage against cost. More resilience and lower latency usually cost more.

questions.q: Which are genuine advantages of building generative AI applications with managed AWS services? Select TWO.
options: Faster time to market
No need to manage the underlying model infrastructure
Models that never produce incorrect answers
No cost until the application reaches one million users
No security responsibilities for the customer at all
notes: Correct. Managed services remove setup work, so teams ship faster.
Correct. AWS runs the servers, scaling, and model hosting.
All models can make mistakes.
Managed services are pay-as-you-go from the first request.
Customers keep responsibility for data, access, and usage.
questions.explain: Advantages include accessibility, lower barrier to entry, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and speed to market. They do not remove model limitations or the customer's share of security responsibility.

questions.q: A team needs full control to run its own open-weight model with custom inference code and a specific GPU instance type. Which AWS service fits better than Amazon Bedrock on-demand?
options: Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Comprehend custom models
AWS Lambda
notes: Correct. SageMaker AI endpoints let you choose the instance type, bring a custom inference container, and run any open-weight model.
Provisioned Throughput reserves Bedrock capacity, but you still cannot choose GPU instances or run custom inference code.
Comprehend custom models are NLP classifiers and entity recognizers, not general LLM hosting.
Lambda does not offer GPU instances and is not designed to host large models.
questions.explain: Rule of thumb: Bedrock for the fastest, fully managed FM access; SageMaker AI for maximum control over models, code, and infrastructure.

questions.q: A product team wants to test models from several providers and switch between them later without rewriting its application. Which Amazon Bedrock characteristic helps most?
options: Access to many providers' models through one consistent API
A single model that cannot be changed after the first deployment
Mandatory fine-tuning before any model can be called
Separate accounts and SDKs required for each model provider
notes: Correct. Bedrock offers models from multiple providers behind a common API (such as the Converse API), so switching is mostly a configuration change.
Bedrock does not lock you into one model.
Base models can be called without any fine-tuning.
Bedrock removes the need for separate provider accounts and SDKs.
questions.explain: Model choice is a key Bedrock benefit: as better or cheaper models appear, you can evaluate and adopt them with little code change.

questions.q: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock being serverless is correct?
options: AWS manages the compute that runs the models; you call an API and pay for usage
You must choose and patch EC2 instances for each model you call
You must install GPU drivers before calling a model
You must build and run your own load balancer in front of every model you want to call
notes: Correct. With serverless Bedrock you never see or manage the underlying instances.
Instance selection and patching apply to self-managed hosting, not Bedrock.
Drivers and hardware are AWS's concern in Bedrock.
Bedrock handles scaling and request routing.
questions.explain: Serverless means no servers for you to provision, scale, or patch. That is a large part of why Bedrock has a low barrier to entry.

questions.q: Match each need to the AWS offering that fits it best.
prompts: Call a foundation model through a managed API with no servers
Deploy and fine-tune an open-weight model on your own SageMaker AI endpoint
Write an agent in a few lines of Python using an open-source SDK
Host and operate agents in production with memory and identity controls
Give business users AI-assisted dashboards, research, and automation
options: Amazon Bedrock
SageMaker JumpStart
Strands Agents
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon Quick
questions.explain: These are the GenAI services listed in skill 2.3.1 of the v1.1 guide. Kiro, the agentic IDE, completes the list.

questions.q: Why might a company choose AWS infrastructure for generative AI because of compliance requirements?
options: AWS services are covered by many third-party compliance programs, and customers can download the audit reports
AWS guarantees that every application a customer builds on AWS is automatically compliant with all laws
Compliance applies only to on-premises systems, so cloud use avoids it entirely
AWS removes the need for customers to document their own AI governance
notes: Correct. AWS maintains certifications and attestations such as SOC, ISO, and PCI, and customers can download the reports through AWS Artifact.
AWS compliance covers its infrastructure; customers must still make their own applications compliant.
Regulations apply wherever data is processed, including the cloud.
Customers remain responsible for their own governance and documentation.
questions.explain: AWS infrastructure offers security, compliance, responsibility (the shared model), and safety benefits. Inherited controls reduce effort, but customer obligations remain.

questions.q: A chatbot gets a mix of simple and complex questions. The team wants Amazon Bedrock to send simple prompts to a smaller, cheaper model and harder prompts to a more capable model in the same family, without writing its own routing logic. Which feature fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing
Amazon Bedrock cross-Region inference
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
Amazon Bedrock model distillation
notes: Correct. Intelligent Prompt Routing predicts response quality for each prompt and routes it to the model that balances quality and cost.
Cross-Region inference spreads traffic across Regions for throughput. It does not choose between models by difficulty.
Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for a model. It does not route between models.
Distillation creates a smaller model ahead of time. It does not route live prompts.
questions.explain: Cost trade-offs (skill 2.3.4) include picking the right model per request. Prompt routing, prompt caching, batch inference, and distillation are the main Bedrock cost levers to know.
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.4; Amazon Bedrock Intelligent Prompt Routing docs

questions.q: An architecture team wants to review its generative AI workload against AWS best practices for security, reliability, cost, and responsible AI, using a structured set of questions. Which AWS offering supports this?
options: The AWS Well-Architected Tool with the Generative AI Lens
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Artifact
Amazon Inspector
notes: Correct. The Well-Architected Tool runs workload reviews, and the Generative AI Lens adds GenAI-specific best practices.
Trusted Advisor checks account settings automatically. It does not run a guided architecture review of a GenAI workload.
Artifact provides AWS compliance reports, not architecture reviews.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities only.
questions.explain: The AWS Well-Architected Tool is in scope. Lenses extend the framework for specific workloads, and the Generative AI Lens covers areas such as model selection, responsible AI, and cost.
questions.ref: Exam guide in-scope services (AWS Well-Architected Tool); Generative AI Lens

questions.q: A team needs licensed third-party datasets, such as financial market data, to enrich a model. It wants to find, subscribe to, and load the data into its AWS account through a managed catalog. Which service fits?
options: AWS Data Exchange
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Macie
AWS Artifact
notes: Correct. AWS Data Exchange lets you find, subscribe to, and use third-party data in the cloud.
DataBrew cleans and prepares data you already have. It does not provide third-party data.
Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. It does not supply datasets.
Artifact provides compliance reports, not datasets.
questions.explain: AWS Data Exchange is an in-scope analytics service. It is a common answer when a scenario needs external, licensed data for analytics or ML.
questions.ref: Exam guide in-scope services (AWS Data Exchange)

questions.q: A startup is comparing serving costs. It expects heavy, steady traffic to a self-hosted open-weight model 24 hours a day and wants the lowest cost per inference on AWS. Which option is designed for this?
options: Amazon EC2 instances with AWS Inferentia chips
Amazon EC2 instances with the largest general-purpose CPUs
AWS Lambda functions with maximum memory
Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
notes: Correct. Inferentia is AWS's purpose-built inference chip, designed for high performance at low cost per inference.
General-purpose CPUs are usually far slower and costlier per inference for large models.
Lambda has no accelerators and is not designed for continuously serving large models.
Glacier is archival storage. It does not serve inference.
questions.explain: AWS infrastructure benefits and cost trade-offs include purpose-built chips: Trainium for training and Inferentia for inference. They also support sustainability through better performance per watt.

questions.q: A company is comparing Amazon Bedrock pricing options for three workloads. Which pairings are correct? Select TWO.
options: Overnight summarization of an archive, with results needed in a day: batch inference
Unpredictable, low traffic for a new prototype: on-demand pay-per-token
Unpredictable, low traffic for a new prototype: a 6-month Provisioned Throughput commitment
A chatbot where every user needs instant answers: batch inference
Overnight summarization of an archive: Provisioned Throughput reserved around the clock
notes: Correct. Batch inference suits large, non-urgent jobs and is priced lower than on-demand for supported models.
Correct. On-demand has no commitment, so it suits low or unpredictable traffic.
A commitment for unpredictable, low traffic means paying for idle capacity.
Batch jobs are asynchronous and cannot give instant answers.
Reserving capacity around the clock for a one-off overnight job wastes money.
questions.explain: Match the pricing model to the workload: on-demand for variable or low traffic, batch for bulk offline work, and Provisioned Throughput for steady, high, or guaranteed capacity (and for some custom models).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 2.3.4; Amazon Bedrock pricing

questions.q: An application uses an FM to extract invoice numbers and totals from emails. The team wants the most consistent, least creative output. How should it set the temperature?
options: Low, close to 0
High, close to 1
Exactly in the middle at 0.5, to balance accuracy and creativity
Temperature does not affect the output
notes: Correct. Low temperature makes the model favor the most likely tokens, which gives focused, repeatable output.
High temperature increases randomness, which is the opposite of what extraction needs.
A middle value still adds randomness that extraction does not need.
Temperature directly controls how random token selection is.
questions.explain: Temperature scales the probability distribution over next tokens. Low values (around 0 to 0.3) suit factual tasks, extraction, and classification. Higher values suit brainstorming and creative writing.

questions.q: A marketing team wants an FM to brainstorm many different and unusual slogan ideas. Which setting change helps most?
options: Increase the temperature
Decrease the maximum output tokens to 5
Set the temperature to 0 so every slogan is the same
Add a stop sequence after the first word of every slogan
notes: Correct. Higher temperature makes less likely tokens more probable, producing more varied and creative output.
Five tokens is too short to write a slogan at all.
Temperature 0 makes outputs as repetitive as possible.
Stopping after one word would cut every slogan off.
questions.explain: Use higher temperature (and possibly higher top-p) for creativity and diversity. The trade-off is more risk of off-topic or incorrect output.

questions.q: What does the top-p (nucleus sampling) parameter control?
options: The model samples only from the most likely tokens whose combined probability reaches p
The percentage of the prompt that the model is allowed to read before it starts writing an answer
The number of parallel requests the endpoint accepts per second
The proportion of training data used to pretrain the model
notes: Correct. With top-p = 0.9, the model picks from the most likely tokens that together make up 90% of the probability mass.
The model always reads the full prompt that fits in its context window.
Throughput limits are a service setting, not a sampling parameter.
Top-p is an inference setting and does not affect training.
questions.explain: Top-p and top-k both limit the pool of candidate tokens. Lower values give more focused output; higher values allow more diversity. Temperature reshapes the probabilities themselves.

questions.q: A model is configured with top-k = 50. What does this mean?
options: At each step the model chooses only among the 50 most likely next tokens
The model returns 50 alternative answers for every prompt
The model may use at most 50 tokens of input per request
The model is automatically retrained on its own outputs after every 50 requests
notes: Correct. Top-k restricts sampling to the k highest-probability tokens at each step.
The number of returned answers is a different setting, if supported at all.
Input length is limited by the context window, not top-k.
Inference never retrains the model.
questions.explain: A smaller top-k (for example 5) makes output more predictable; a larger top-k allows more variety. It is often combined with temperature and top-p.

questions.q: Users report that the assistant's long answers stop abruptly in the middle of a sentence. Which inference parameter should the team check first?
options: Maximum output tokens (response length limit)
Temperature
Top-k
The embedding model used by the knowledge base for retrieval
notes: Correct. If max tokens is too low, generation stops when the limit is reached, even mid-sentence.
Temperature affects randomness, not where output stops.
Top-k limits candidate tokens, not output length.
The embedding model affects retrieval quality, not truncated answers.
questions.explain: Output length settings control cost and latency, but setting them too low truncates answers. Balance the limit against what the task needs.

questions.q: A developer wants the model to stop generating as soon as it writes the text 'END_OF_ANSWER'. Which parameter does this?
options: A stop sequence
Top-p
Temperature
Provisioned Throughput
notes: Correct. Stop sequences tell the model to stop generating when it produces a specified string.
Top-p controls which tokens may be sampled.
Temperature controls randomness.
Provisioned Throughput is a capacity and pricing option.
questions.explain: Stop sequences help keep outputs in a fixed format and avoid wasted tokens, for example by stopping after one item in a list.

questions.q: Match each inference parameter to its effect.
prompts: Higher values make output more random and creative
Limits sampling to the most likely tokens up to a cumulative probability
Caps how long the generated response can be
Ends generation when a chosen string appears
options: Temperature
Top-p
Maximum output tokens
Stop sequence
questions.explain: These parameters let you tune the same model for different tasks without retraining: low temperature for precise answers, length limits for cost control, and stop sequences for structured output.

questions.q: What is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
options: Retrieving relevant information from a knowledge source and adding it to the prompt to ground the answer
Retraining the FM's weights every night on all of the newly uploaded company documents
Generating synthetic training data for a supervised learning model
Compressing a large model into a smaller one that runs faster and costs less to host
notes: Correct. RAG grounds the model's answer in retrieved content, without changing the model.
Changing the weights is fine-tuning or continued pretraining, not RAG.
Synthetic data generation is a different technique.
Compressing a model is distillation or quantization.
questions.explain: RAG retrieves relevant chunks (usually by vector similarity) and places them in the prompt. It lets an FM use private and up-to-date information, reduces hallucinations, and supports citations.

questions.q: An electronics retailer updates its product specifications and prices every day. It wants an FM assistant that always answers using current information. What is the best approach?
options: RAG over the latest product data
Fine-tune the model once on last year's product catalog
Pretrain a new model from scratch every week
Rely on the FM's built-in knowledge from pretraining
notes: Correct. RAG retrieves today's data at question time, so answers stay current without retraining.
A one-time fine-tune quickly goes stale as products change.
Weekly pretraining from scratch would be extremely expensive and slow.
Pretraining knowledge has a cutoff date and knows nothing about this retailer's catalog.
questions.explain: Choose RAG when knowledge changes often, must be traceable to sources, or is private. Fine-tuning is better for changing style, format, or task behavior, not for keeping facts current.

questions.q: A company stores its HR policies as PDFs in Amazon S3. It wants a managed way to build RAG on them, including chunking, embeddings, a vector store, and retrieval, with minimal code. Which AWS capability fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Bedrock Agents
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
notes: Correct. Knowledge Bases ingests from S3, chunks, embeds, stores vectors, and retrieves them, all managed.
Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks and tools. They can use a knowledge base, but they do not build the RAG pipeline.
JumpStart deploys models to endpoints. You would still have to build chunking, embedding, and retrieval yourself.
Prompt Management stores and versions prompts. It does not ingest or retrieve documents.
questions.explain: Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability in Amazon Bedrock. You choose the data source, embedding model, chunking strategy, and vector store (or let it create one).
questions.ref: Exam guide skill 3.1.3 (Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases)

questions.q: Put the steps of answering a user's question with RAG in order.
options: The user submits a question
The question is converted into an embedding
The most similar chunks are retrieved from the vector store
The retrieved chunks are added to the prompt with the question
The foundation model generates an answer grounded in those chunks
questions.explain: At query time, RAG embeds the question, finds nearby chunk vectors, augments the prompt with those chunks, and lets the FM generate a grounded answer, often with citations.

questions.q: Put the steps of preparing documents for a RAG knowledge base in order.
options: Load the source documents from the data source
Split the documents into chunks
Generate an embedding for each chunk
Store the embeddings in a vector store
questions.explain: Ingestion turns documents into searchable vectors: load, chunk, embed, store. Bedrock Knowledge Bases runs this pipeline for you and can re-sync when the source data changes.
